title: Mudra SDK — Account Sign-In & Licensing
text:
Mudra SDK — Account Sign-In & Licensing ¶ If you are building an app on top of this SDK, read this page before you
skip sign-in as “optional polish.” Connecting to a device never requires
an account — a signed-out app still connects and streams fine. But every
device enforces a capability tier ( FREE / PLUS / PRO ) via a signed license
token, and higher-tier features stay locked unless something provisions
that token onto the device — for example, on a Mudra Pro the highest EMG
ODR allowed is 200 SPS on FREE , 800 on PLUS and 6400 on PRO (a higher set_emg_odr is rejected with ERR_LICENSE ), and SD-card recording needs PRO . If your app
never calls into mudra_sdk.auth , your users are silently capped at
whatever tier their device already happens to hold — usually FREE — even
if their account is entitled to more. A real app needs a sign-in flow; a
one-off script usually doesn’t. Two independent pieces ¶ The SDK splits this into two orthogonal halves — you can use either without
the other: mudra_sdk.auth — account sign-in against the Mudra cloud, and
pushing a tier-appropriate license token down to a connected device. Device-level license query/apply ( MudraDevice methods) — reads or
sets whatever token is already on the device, with no account
involved. 1. Account sign-in ( mudra_sdk.auth ) ¶ import asyncio from mudra_sdk import auth # Sign in BEFORE connecting. sign_in_email is blocking HTTP, so run it off the loop. tier = await asyncio . to_thread ( auth . sign_in_email , "user@example.com" , "password" ) # "FREE"/"PLUS"/"PRO" await device . connect () # signed in -> the SDK provisions license + user_id itself # Only if you signed in AFTER the device was already connected: await auth . provision_device ( device ) # fetches a token from the server, sends it await auth . provision_user_id ( device ) auth . logout () # forgets the in-memory tier/user ref; stored cloud tokens stay (see below) sign_in_email is a synchronous, blocking HTTP call — from async code,
run it via await asyncio.to_thread(...) so it doesn’t stall the event
loop. It raises requests.HTTPError on failure (bad credentials, no
connectivity, unactivated account); a try / except around it is how you
surface a sign-in error to a user. Provisioning is automatic. If you’re signed in when a device
connects, the SDK itself runs auth.provision_device(device) and auth.provision_user_id(device) on every connect, and LicenseManager (below) renews the license before it expires. So sign in before connecting. Call those two yourself only if you signed in after the device
was already connected (or reconnect it instead). Both are no-ops when
signed out, so calling them is always safe. What’s kept where. The signed-in tier and user ref live in memory
only, per process — after a restart, the SDK provisions nothing until you
call sign_in_email again. But the cloud client stores the access token,
refresh token and email on disk in ~/.mudra_sdk/auth_storage.json , and auth.logout() doesn’t clear that file — so MudraServerClient calls
keep working after logout and in a new process. For a
full sign-out, also clear the stored tokens: from mudra_sdk.cloud import AuthStorage auth . logout () AuthStorage () . clear () Reference implementation: the example app’s sign-in bar is a thin Tkinter
wrapper over sign_in_email / logout — examples/mudra_connect/panels/auth.py . 2. Device-level license query/apply ¶ Independent of any account, you can always ask a connected device what
license it’s currently carrying, or set one directly: await device . set_on_license_device_info_received ( lambda info : print ( f "tier= { info . tier . name } valid= { info . valid } serial= { info . serial } " ) ) await device . get_device_info () # -> LicenseDeviceInfo via the callback above (BLE + CDC) await device . apply_license ( "<88-byte token as hex>" ) # set directly, bypassing auth.py await device . clear_license () # drop to FREE LicenseDeviceInfo fields: tier (a LicenseTier enum — FREE / PLUS / PRO ; print .name ), valid (bool), now / floor / expires_at (unix
seconds, anti-rollback bookkeeping), serial (str). get_device_info() / apply_license() / clear_license() work on both BLE
and CDC, including decoding the reply into LicenseDeviceInfo . The last
reply is cached in device.get_license_device_info() . Keeping a license alive: LicenseManager ¶ A license token has an expiry window. For a long-running connection, MudraDevice owns a LicenseManager (one per device, started on connect, stopped on disconnect) that re-queries
the device’s license every 5 minutes and, once a valid license has less than
7 minutes left, re-provisions it — so a session that outlives the token
doesn’t silently drop back to a lower tier mid-use. It runs on its own; you
don’t need to call anything for it. Renewal fetches a fresh token from the server, so it only works while
signed in — signed out, it does nothing. A token you applied manually with apply_license() isn’t renewed on its own terms: if you’re signed in, the
renewal replaces it with your account’s token; if not, it simply expires. user_id provisioning (SD-card recording) ¶ SD-card recording (see SENSORS.md §5 )
needs a 16-byte user_id set on the device before it’ll start — this is
handled automatically, the same way license provisioning is: During every connect, the SDK sends the signed-in account’s identifier
to the device as its user_id — no call needed on your part. Sign in before connecting for this to take effect; signing in after a device is
already connected does not push it — reconnect the device (or call await auth.provision_user_id(device) yourself) instead. Signed out at connect time, nothing is sent — set_storage_record() then fails with BtCmdStatus.ERR_STATE until a user_id is set: sign in
and reconnect (or call auth.provision_user_id(device) ), or call device.set_user_id(...) yourself with exactly 16 bytes. auth.get_user_ref() returns the raw value if you need it for your own
purposes (e.g. logging); most apps never need to call it. Practical checklist for an app built on this SDK ¶ Add a sign-in UI (email/password at minimum — see panels/auth.py for a
minimal example) unless you specifically want to ship a tool that only
ever uses whatever tier a device already has. Sign in before connecting — the SDK then provisions the license and user_id on every connect and keeps the license renewed. If the user
signs in while a device is already connected, call await auth.provision_device(device) and await auth.provision_user_id(device) (or reconnect). Call sign_in_email off the event loop ( await asyncio.to_thread(...) )
— it’s blocking HTTP. Surface the device’s actual tier back to the user via set_on_license_device_info_received , rather than assuming sign-in
succeeded means the device is licensed — the two are asynchronous and
independent. After a restart, the user must sign in again before devices get
provisioned (the tier is memory-only), even though the stored cloud
tokens survive. If your app offers “sign out”, clear those too
( auth.logout() plus AuthStorage().clear() ). See also: CONNECTION.md §5 for
this material in the context of the full connect/scan/ping flow.

title: Mudra SDK — Callbacks Reference
text:
Mudra SDK — Callbacks Reference ¶ Part of the Mudra SDK usage guide . See also: CONNECTION.md · SENSORS.md The SDK has exactly two kinds of callback: The global MudraDelegate (§1) — one instance for the whole
process, registered once via Mudra().set_delegate(...) . Reports device
discovery and connection lifecycle for every device. Per-device set_on_* callbacks (§2) — registered on a specific MudraDevice . Reports sensor data, status, storage, licensing, errors,
and ping for that device only. Every callback must be a plain def function — delegate methods and
per-device callbacks alike. The SDK calls them directly on the asyncio loop
thread without awaiting them, so an async def callback never actually runs.
Keep them fast; if you need to do async work in response, schedule it with asyncio.create_task(...) . Every per-device setter is async and fire-and-forget — await device.set_on_x(fn) just stores fn ; it doesn’t itself trigger anything
(except the sensor-streaming setters in §2.1, where setting the callback is the enable/disable action — see SENSORS.md ).
Pass None to unregister. 1. MudraDelegate (global, one per process) ¶ from mudra_sdk.models.callbacks import MudraDelegate from mudra_sdk.models.mudra_device import MudraDevice class MyDelegate ( MudraDelegate ): def on_device_discovered ( self , device : MudraDevice ): ... def on_mudra_device_connecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): ... def on_mudra_device_connected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): ... def on_mudra_device_disconnecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): ... def on_mudra_device_disconnected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): ... def on_mudra_device_connection_failed ( self , device : MudraDevice , error : str ): ... def on_bluetooth_state_changed ( self , state : bool ): ... Mudra () . set_delegate ( MyDelegate ()) All seven methods are abstract — you must implement every one (it’s an
ABC), as plain def methods. The example app’s delegate.py is a good template. Method Fires when on_device_discovered(device) A device (BLE or CDC) is found by scan_ble() / scan_cdc() or returned by get_connected_devices() . Fires once per address per scan session; restarting a scan, a change in a CDC device’s port info, or get_connected_devices() can report the same address again — always with the same MudraDevice object. on_mudra_device_connecting(device) Right after device.connect() is called, before the transport handshake starts. on_mudra_device_connected(device) The link is open (BLE: GATT connected; CDC: both ports opened and handshaken) — before the SDK’s own setup (BLE: notification subscriptions and initial queries; CDC: status queries and START ). Not the “ready” signal: the device is ready when await device.connect() returns. See SDK_USAGE.md §4 . on_mudra_device_disconnecting(device) Right after device.disconnect() is called on a connected device, before teardown. Not fired for an unexpected drop. on_mudra_device_disconnected(device) Teardown complete — for either a caller-initiated disconnect or an unexpected drop (BLE radio loss, USB unplug). No separate callback for “lost connection” vs. “I disconnected it.” on_mudra_device_connection_failed(device, error) connect() failed (it doesn’t raise); error is a human-readable message. If a CDC device’s USB cable is pulled mid-connect, this is followed by on_mudra_device_disconnected . On BLE it can come after on_mudra_device_connected if GATT setup fails once the link is open — the SDK then disconnects ( disconnecting / disconnected fire) and reports the failure. on_bluetooth_state_changed(state) Never fired by the SDK today. You must implement it (it’s abstract), but don’t rely on it. This is a single global delegate for all devices — every callback
receives the specific device it’s about, so multi-device apps dispatch on device.address (or device is my_device ) inside these methods rather
than registering one delegate per device. 2. Per-device callbacks ¶ Registered on a device: MudraDevice via await device.set_on_<name>(callback_or_none) . When to register. The status, storage, licensing, firmware-version,
error, ping and battery callbacks (§2.2–§2.5) just store your function, so
you can register them before calling connect() — they stay registered
until the next disconnect (§3) — or from on_mudra_device_connected . Doing
it before connect() returns is how you catch the replies to the SDK’s own
connect-time queries. The streaming setters (§2.1) send a power command, so
call them only after await device.connect() has returned. 2.1 Sensor streaming callbacks ¶ Enabling the sensor’s data stream is setting one of these (see SENSORS.md §1 ): Setter Callback signature set_on_emg_ready (timestamp: int, samples: list[float], frequency: int, frequency_std: float) -> None set_on_imu_h_ready same signature set_on_imu_f_ready same signature set_on_ppg_h_ready same signature (hand PPG, 2 channels) set_on_ppg_f_ready same signature (finger/ring PPG, 2 channels; silent while the ring is disconnected) 2.2 Sensor status callbacks ¶ Fired on reply to get_<sensor>_status() and on unsolicited firmware
pushes after a config change (see SENSORS.md §2 ): Setter Callback argument set_on_emg_status_received EmgStatus set_on_h_imu_status_received ImuStatus set_on_f_imu_status_received ImuStatus set_on_ppg_h_status_received PpgStatus set_on_ppg_f_status_received PpgStatus 2.3 Storage / SD recording callbacks (BLE only) ¶ See SENSORS.md §5 . Setter Callback argument set_on_storage_record_state_received RecordStatus set_on_storage_record_error_received BtCmdStatus set_on_storage_next_file_num_received int (next free file number) 2.3b Licensing & firmware version (BLE + CDC) ¶ See CONNECTION.md §5 . Setter Callback argument Fires on set_on_license_device_info_received LicenseDeviceInfo ( .tier is a LicenseTier enum — print .name ) Reply to device.get_device_info() , including the SDK’s own connect-time query and LicenseManager ’s periodic checks. Last value cached in device.get_license_device_info() . set_on_firmware_version_received FirmwareVersion ( .major / .minor / .patch / .tweak ; .version_string → "X.Y.Z.W" ) Reply to device.get_firmware_version() — the SDK queries it on every connect. Last value cached in device.get_firmware_version_info() . Over CDC the firmware reports only X.Y.Z , so .tweak is 0 . 2.4 Errors ¶ Setter Callback argument Fires on set_on_command_error_received (cmd_id: BtCmdId, status: BtCmdStatus) Any non-OK status-only reply — failed enable/disable, failed SET, RECORD_SET rejected, etc. Also fires for async STORAGE_RECORD_ERROR pushes, and (CDC) immediately for any storage/SD call, with ERR_UNKNOWN . Over CDC there are no numeric status codes: the firmware replies <TOKEN> ERROR <reason> , and the SDK maps the reason to a BtCmdStatus — running → ERR_BUSY (config change on a running sensor), license / bind / expired → ERR_LICENSE , format → ERR_INVALID , internal → ERR_INTERNAL , anything else → ERR_UNKNOWN . Only replies whose token maps
to a subsystem ( EMG… , H_IMU… , F_IMU… , PPG_H… , PPG_F… , BAT… , LED… , BT… , LICENSE… ) reach this callback; other error replies are only logged. 2.5 Connectivity / device state ¶ Setter Callback argument Fires on set_on_ping_response (no arguments) Reply to device.ping() — see CONNECTION.md §3 . set_on_charging_state_changed is_charging: bool BLE: GATT notification on the battery power-state characteristic. CDC: MudraDevice polls BAT_CHG? at connect and every 30 s (no push exists on that transport) and feeds the reply through this same callback. set_on_battery_level_changed level: int BLE: GATT notification on the battery characteristic. CDC: polled via BAT_SOC? alongside set_on_charging_state_changed above. 2.6 Checking whether a callback is currently registered ¶ Every setter above has a matching is_on_<name>_callback_set() -> bool getter, e.g.: device . is_on_emg_ready_callback_set () device . is_on_ppg_h_status_received_callback_set () device . is_on_command_error_received_callback_set () Useful for UI code that needs to reflect current state (e.g. an
Enable/Disable toggle button) without keeping its own shadow copy of what
was registered. 3. Callbacks don’t survive a disconnect ¶ device.disconnect() (and an unexpected drop) clears most per-device
callbacks automatically — handle_disconnection() resets: All five streaming callbacks (§2.1) All five status callbacks (§2.2) All three storage callbacks (§2.3) The license-info and firmware-version callbacks (§2.3b) The command-error callback (§2.4) The ping-response callback (§2.5) It also resets the cached values behind get_*_status_info() , get_record_status_info() , get_next_file_num_info() , get_license_device_info() and get_firmware_version_info() to None , and
zeroes the packet-loss counters. Not cleared: set_on_charging_state_changed and set_on_battery_level_changed — those two persist across a
disconnect/reconnect cycle. Practical effect: if you reconnect the same MudraDevice object after a
disconnect, re-register every callback in §2.1–§2.4 and the ping callback
— don’t assume they’re still wired up from before. Charging/battery
callbacks are the one exception and don’t need re-registering.

title: Mudra SDK — Connection Guide (Scan, BLE, CDC)
text:
Mudra SDK — Connection Guide (Scan, BLE, CDC) ¶ Part of the Mudra SDK usage guide . See also: SENSORS.md · CALLBACKS.md Covers finding a device (§1), connecting/disconnecting over either transport
(§2), the round-trip ping check (§3), sending raw commands (§4),
licensing/account sign-in (§5), firmware update (§6), connection-specific
pitfalls (§7), and connecting to more than one device at once (§8). Assumes you already have a Mudra() singleton and a registered MudraDelegate — see SDK_USAGE.md for
setup and CALLBACKS.md for the full delegate reference. 1. Scanning ¶ BLE and CDC scanning are started and stopped independently — call whichever
transport(s) you actually need: mudra = Mudra () await mudra . scan_ble () # BleService.scan(), non-blocking await mudra . scan_cdc () # CdcService.scan(), non-blocking ... await mudra . stop_scan_ble () await mudra . stop_scan_cdc () Mudra.scan_ble() fires BleService.scan() (continuous BleakScanner ,
keeps advertisements whose name contains "Mudra Pro" or "Mudra Ultimate" — that name also picks the model). Mudra.scan_cdc() fires CdcService.scan() (polls serial.tools.list_ports every 2s for USB VID/PID 0x2FE3 / 0x0001 —
shared by both models — probing each candidate COM port with a CDC? handshake to tell the CONFIG and DATA ports apart, then a TSYNC? probe to tell Pro from Ultimate). A CDC device’s address is its USB
serial number (or a port name, if the device reports no serial number). Run both concurrently if you want devices from either
transport — they report through the same delegate callback either way. Each discovered device — BLE or CDC — triggers one call to MudraDelegate.on_device_discovered(device: MudraDevice) per address per
scan session; repeats within a session are de-duplicated internally. The
same address can be reported again when you restart a scan, when a CDC
device’s port info changes (e.g. its DATA port finishes enumerating), or
by get_connected_devices() — you get the same MudraDevice object
each time, so de-duplicate on the object or device.address if that
matters to you. The same physical device seen over BLE and USB is two separate MudraDevice objects (BLE address vs. USB serial number), each with its own
connection. Firmware update needs the CDC one (§6). Each transport’s scan keeps running until you call its own stop_scan_ble() / stop_scan_cdc() ; it does not auto-stop after finding a
device, and stopping one transport’s scan has no effect on the other’s. To find devices that are already connected (e.g. a previous process
left a BLE connection open), use: devices = await mudra . get_connected_devices () This also fires on_device_discovered for each one, same as scan. A BLE
device found this way still needs await device.connect() in this process
before you can use it (the CDC devices it returns are just the ones this
process already has open). 2. Connecting / disconnecting (BLE and CDC) ¶ Both directions work identically regardless of transport — call it either
on the device or through Mudra() ; they’re equivalent: await device . connect () # == await Mudra().connect(device); never raises await device . disconnect () # == await Mudra().disconnect(device) is_up = await Mudra () . is_connected ( device ) connect() doesn’t raise on failure — the failure arrives via MudraDelegate.on_mudra_device_connection_failed , so check await Mudra().is_connected(device) after it returns. When it returns with
the device connected, the SDK’s connect sequence (below) is done and you can
enable sensors. What “connect” does, per transport: BLE CDC (USB serial) Underlying call BleakClient.connect() + GATT service/characteristic discovery, subscribes to notifications Opens the CONFIG serial port, handshakes with CDC? , opens+handshakes the DATA port, starts a background reader thread Setup before connect() returns Once the COMMAND characteristic is found, the SDK sends the initial sensor-status, license and user_id queries/provisioning device.on_cdc_ready() (queries EMG/H_IMU/F_IMU/PPG_H/PPG_F status and battery, starts license/ user_id provisioning) then device.start_streaming() (sends START ) — CDC’s DATA port is silent until this on_mudra_device_connected fires As soon as the link is up — before notifications are subscribed As soon as both ports are open — before the status queries and START Data delivery GATT notifications on the DATA characteristic Background thread reading the DATA serial port Disconnect Unsubscribes/ BleakClient.disconnect() Sends STOP , closes both serial ports, joins reader thread You normally don’t need to think about any of this — it’s handled inside connect() / disconnect() . It matters mainly for understanding when sensor data starts flowing (CDC needs the explicit START , which the SDK
sends for you before connect() returns). Over BLE, the replies to the
initial queries arrive asynchronously after connect() returns; over CDC
they’re read back before it returns — so register status callbacks before
calling connect() if you want to see them (see CALLBACKS.md §2 ). Unexpected disconnects (BLE radio drop, USB unplug) are detected by the
transport and reported through the same MudraDelegate.on_mudra_device_disconnected callback — you don’t need a
separate error path for “lost connection” vs. “I called disconnect()”. Over
CDC this also covers an unplug while connecting : after connecting fires,
a detach always ends in on_mudra_device_disconnected (preceded by on_mudra_device_connection_failed if the ports hadn’t finished opening). Note
that disconnecting (expected or not) clears most per-device callbacks on
that MudraDevice — see the “callbacks don’t survive a disconnect” note in CALLBACKS.md . Transport differences to know about: CDC has no PING firmware token; device.ping() substitutes the CDC? handshake as a round-trip probe and still fires the set_on_ping_response callback on success (§3 below). CDC has no SD-card storage/recording protocol at all — see SENSORS.md . Raw commands: BLE takes binary frames, CDC takes ASCII lines — see §4
below. 3. Ping / round-trip check ¶ await device . set_on_ping_response ( lambda : print ( "pong" )) await device . ping () ping() sends a single request ( SYSTEM_PING over BLE, the CDC? handshake over CDC as a substitute) — timing/repetition is on you. Nothing
fires on failure or timeout: the callback only runs when a reply arrives, so
implement your own timeout (e.g. wait on an asyncio.Event set from the
callback with asyncio.wait_for ). The
reference app’s repeating ping-and-measure-latency loop lives entirely at
the app layer, not in the SDK — see panels/ping.py . 4. Raw / advanced commands ¶ For anything not covered by a typed wrapper method: await device . send_command ( bytes ([ ... ])) # BLE only — raw binary CONFIG frame await Mudra () . send_cdc_command ( device , "EMG_ODR?" ) # CDC only — raw ASCII CONFIG line Both return None — there’s no reply value. Over CDC, a reply that maps to
a typed event is routed to the matching callback (sensor status lines to the
status callbacks, <TOKEN> ERROR ... lines to the command-error callback,
plus device-info/firmware-version/battery replies); anything else (a plain <TOKEN> OK ack or a parameter GET reply) is only written to the debug log. The advanced/raw-command panel in the example app
( panels/command.py )
branches on device.transport for exactly this reason — pick the binary or
ASCII path depending on which transport device is on. device.CMD is the device’s own command table — ProFirmwareCommand on a MudraPro , UltimateFirmwareCommand on a MudraUltimate (both in mudra_sdk.models.enums ; the two tables are independent). Each member has an .op_code , a .description , and .id — the BLE byte template for that
command (e.g. bytes(device.CMD.systemPing.id) ); useful for building your
own frames or logging. 5. Licensing & account sign-in ¶ Building an app, not just a script? See AUTH.md for why
sign-in matters (tier-gated features silently stay locked without it),
the full API, and a practical checklist. This section is the short
version. The device enforces a capability tier ( FREE / PLUS / PRO ) via a signed
license token. The SDK has two independent, orthogonal pieces for this —
you can use either without the other: import asyncio from mudra_sdk import auth # Sign in BEFORE connecting: every later connect then provisions the device # (license token + user_id) automatically, and LicenseManager renews it. tier = await asyncio . to_thread ( auth . sign_in_email , "user@example.com" , "password" ) # "FREE"/"PLUS"/"PRO" await device . connect () # Only if you signed in AFTER the device was already connected: await auth . provision_device ( device ) # fetches a token from the server, sends it await auth . provision_user_id ( device ) auth . logout () # forgets the in-memory tier; stored cloud tokens stay on disk (see AUTH.md) Connecting to a device never requires an account; signed out, it just uses
whatever tier is already on it, and provision_device() / provision_user_id() are no-ops. The signed-in tier lives in memory for the current process only,
but the cloud client’s access/refresh tokens are stored on disk and logout() doesn’t clear them — see AUTH.md . Independent of sign-in, query what’s actually on the device right now: await device . set_on_license_device_info_received ( lambda info : print ( f "tier= { info . tier . name } valid= { info . valid } serial= { info . serial } " ) ) await device . get_device_info () # -> LicenseDeviceInfo via the callback above (BLE + CDC) await device . apply_license ( "<88-byte token as hex>" ) # set directly, bypassing auth.py await device . clear_license () # drop to FREE LicenseDeviceInfo fields: tier (a LicenseTier enum — FREE / PLUS / PRO ; use .name to print it), valid (bool), now / floor / expires_at (unix seconds, anti-rollback bookkeeping), serial (str). get_device_info() / apply_license() / clear_license() work on both BLE and
CDC, and the reply decodes into LicenseDeviceInfo on both. The last one
received is also cached in device.get_license_device_info() . 6. Firmware update (DFU, USB only) ¶ from mudra_sdk.service import DfuError , DfuStage def on_stage ( stage : str ) -> None : print ( stage ) # one of DfuStage.CONNECT / UPLOAD / MARK / RESET / DONE def on_progress ( offset : int , total : int ) -> None : print ( f " { offset } / { total } bytes" ) try : version = await device . start_dfu ( # `device` must be the CDC (USB) MudraDevice "app_flpr.signed.bin" , on_progress = on_progress , on_stage = on_stage ) print ( f "staged firmware v { version } — device is rebooting" ) except DfuError as e : # failed after the SMP port was found print ( f "failed at stage { e . stage } : { e . message } " ) except RuntimeError as e : # no CDC identity, or no SMP port found print ( f "can't start firmware update: { e } " ) USB (CDC) only — device.start_dfu(...) raises RuntimeError immediately
if device has no CDC identity ( device.as_cdc_device() is None ), whether
or not it’s currently connected via CDC — there is no BLE DFU transport on
either product yet. A device you found over BLE is a different MudraDevice object from the same device found over USB (§1); scan with scan_cdc() and
use that one. Requires DFU-enabled firmware already running on the device — this
updates firmware, it doesn’t install DFU support onto a device that lacks
it. The SDK finds the device’s SMP port itself (a third USB-CDC-ACM port,
separate from CONFIG / DATA , confirmed with an MCUmgr echo round-trip) —
if no such port exists, start_dfu() raises RuntimeError with a message
to that effect. Flow : connect to the SMP port → upload the signed image → mark it
pending (test-swap, not confirmed) → reset. MCUboot swaps and boots the new
image on its own after reset — there is no device-side “update complete”
push, so reconnect afterward to confirm the new version actually landed. start_dfu() returns the staged image’s version string, not a
post-reboot confirmation. on_stage / on_progress are both optional and fire synchronously from
inside the coroutine (not through the global MudraDelegate or a set_on_* callback) — on_stage(stage: str) with one of DfuStage.CONNECT / .UPLOAD / .MARK / .RESET / .DONE ; on_progress(offset: int, total: int) fires repeatedly during .UPLOAD only. Errors : a missing CDC identity or missing SMP port raises plain RuntimeError ; anything that fails after the SMP port is found (connect,
upload, mark, reset) raises DfuError (from mudra_sdk.service ), whose .stage / .message attributes identify which step failed. DfuError is a
subclass of RuntimeError , so catch it first (as above). A bad firmware
path raises FileNotFoundError / OSError before anything is sent. See panels/dfu.py for the
reference app’s firmware-update tab. 7. Connection pitfalls ¶ Calling sensor/config/storage methods before the device is connected — every method sends over the live transport; there’s no queuing. Wait
for await device.connect() to return, then confirm with await Mudra().is_connected(device) . Treating on_mudra_device_connected as “ready” — it fires as soon as
the link is open, before the SDK’s setup (BLE notifications, CDC status
queries and START ). The ready point is await device.connect() returning — see the note in SDK_USAGE.md . Expecting connect() to raise — it doesn’t; failures arrive via on_mudra_device_connection_failed . Check is_connected() afterwards. Expecting ping() to report a failure — nothing fires on timeout;
implement your own (§3). CDC-only gaps — no SD storage/recording, no PING token (use ping() , which substitutes CDC? ), raw commands are ASCII text not
binary bytes. One global delegate — MudraDelegate callbacks aren’t scoped to a
device; check device.address / device is my_device inside them if you
manage more than one device at a time. 8. Multiple devices at once ¶ Nothing about the SDK is single-device — Mudra() keeps every discovered MudraDevice in an internal {address: MudraDevice} registry and dispatches
every transport event (data, status, storage, errors, ping, battery,
device info) by looking up the target device from that registry, so several
devices — BLE, CDC, or a mix — can be connected and streaming
simultaneously within one process: mudra = Mudra () await mudra . scan_ble () await mudra . scan_cdc () # ... on_device_discovered fires once per address; connect to as many as you want ... await device_a . connect () await device_b . connect () await device_a . set_on_emg_ready ( lambda * args : handle ( device_a , * args )) await device_b . set_on_emg_ready ( lambda * args : handle ( device_b , * args )) Each MudraDevice ’s per-device callbacks (§2.1–§2.5 in CALLBACKS.md ) are independent — registering one doesn’t
affect any other device. The global MudraDelegate is shared across every device — its
callbacks always receive the specific device the event is about, so
dispatch on device.address (or device is my_device ) inside them rather
than assuming a single device’s worth of state. There’s no built-in cap on how many devices you can hold connected at
once — the practical limit is your BLE adapter’s own connection count and
how many USB-CDC ports you have wired up, not anything in this SDK. The Mudra Connect example app works this way: each connected device gets its
own window and state, opened and closed from the delegate’s connection
callbacks — see device_window.py and delegate.py .

title: Mudra SDK — Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) Guide
text:
Mudra SDK — Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) Guide ¶ Part of the Mudra SDK usage guide . See also: SENSORS.md · CALLBACKS.md · data_format.md Lab Streaming Layer is the standard way
research labs record several devices on one timeline: each device publishes
its data as named streams on the local network, and a recorder such as LabRecorder saves them
all — a Mudra band, an EEG cap, an eye tracker — into one .xdf file. mudra_sdk.lsl publishes a connected Mudra Pro or Mudra Ultimate device’s
sensors as LSL streams, one stream per sensor. It is a thin layer on top of the
SDK’s per-sensor streaming callbacks
( SENSORS.md §1 ), with no
device I/O of its own, so BLE and USB-CDC, Mudra Pro and Mudra Ultimate all
work the same. mudra_sdk/lsl/
  bridge.py      MudraLslBridge — the part you use
  clock.py       DeviceClockMapper — device timestamps -> LSL time
  metadata.py    stream names, channel labels and units
examples/
  lsl_app.py     command-line streamer: `python examples/lsl_app.py` (§2)
  mudra_lsl/     the CLI itself (cli.py) 1. Install ¶ pylsl is an optional dependency — nothing else in the SDK needs it, and import mudra_sdk.lsl works without it. Only MudraLslBridge.start() does: pip install pylsl pylsl includes the native liblsl library on Windows and macOS. On Linux,
install liblsl separately (your distro’s package, or a release from sccn/liblsl ). 2. Quickstart ¶ Connect as usual and check that it connected: start the bridge after await device.connect() has returned and await Mudra().is_connected(device) is true — not from on_mudra_device_connected , which fires before the SDK has
finished setting the device up (see SDK_USAGE.md §4 ). Then hand the
device to a MudraLslBridge : import asyncio from mudra_sdk.lsl import MudraLslBridge async def stream ( device ): # `device` is a connected MudraDevice (MudraPro or MudraUltimate, BLE or CDC) async with MudraLslBridge ( device , device_id = "band0" ) as bridge : print ( bridge . streams ) # On a Mudra Pro (no finger IMU) with no ring connected, imu_ring and # ppg_f are in bridge.skipped: # {'emg': 'MudraPro-band0-EMG', 'imu_hand': 'MudraPro-band0-IMU_HAND', #  'ppg_h': 'MudraPro-band0-PPG_H'} await asyncio . sleep ( 60 ) # the sensors are on and live on LSL # leaving the block turns the sensors off and closes the streams await device . disconnect () Open LabRecorder on any machine on the same network, and the streams appear in
its list. Without async with , call start() and stop() yourself — put stop() in a finally block, so the sensors are turned off even on errors (§4): async def stream ( device ): bridge = MudraLslBridge ( device , sensors = [ "emg" , "imu_hand" ]) await bridge . start () try : ... finally : await bridge . stop () await device . disconnect () Argument Default Meaning device — A connected MudraDevice . device_id device serial, else its name Label in every stream name. Must differ per device when you stream several. sensors all five Any of "emg" , "imu_hand" , "imu_ring" , "ppg_h" , "ppg_f" — which sensors to publish and turn on . status_timeout 3.0 Seconds start() waits for each sensor’s status reply. From the command line ¶ examples/lsl_app.py does all of the above with no code: it finds a device,
connects, and publishes its sensors until you press Ctrl-C (run it from the
repo root; the source is examples/mudra_lsl/cli.py ): python examples / lsl_app . py # first device found, all sensors python examples / lsl_app . py -- transport ble -- name 48 - 25 # a specific BLE device python examples / lsl_app . py -- transport cdc -- sensors emg imu_hand -- duration 60 python examples / lsl_app . py -- emg - odr 3200 -- emg - res 24 -- device - id band0 python examples / lsl_app . py -- list # list the devices found, then exit Run python examples/lsl_app.py --help for every option. Worth knowing: Devices already connected to the computer are found first. A band paired
to a Windows PC is connected by Windows automatically and stops advertising,
so a scan alone never finds it; the CLI asks Mudra.get_connected_devices() ( CONNECTION.md §1 ) before scanning. Signing in is optional, but it decides the tier ( AUTH.md ). Without an account the device streams at whatever tier
it already holds. Pass --email / --password (or set MUDRA_EMAIL / MUDRA_PASSWORD ) and the device gets the account’s tier on connect — needed
for higher ODRs and 24-bit EMG. --emg-odr , --emg-res , --imu-odr and --ppg-odr are applied after
connecting and before any sensor is turned on, as SENSORS.md §3 requires. --emg-odr is checked against the connected model’s rates. --ppg-odr sets the PPG chip’s one ODR, shared by ppg_h and ppg_f . The CLI exits with status 1 if the device disconnects while streaming. 3. What it publishes ¶ One stream per sensor. An LSL stream has one fixed sample rate and channel
count, so the sensors can’t share one. Both are read from the device’s status
when the bridge starts, never hard-coded: Sensor key Stream name LSL type Channels Units emg MudraPro-<device_id>-EMG EMG ch0 … chN — 3 on Pro, 8 on Ultimate normalized (about −1…1) imu_hand MudraPro-<device_id>-IMU_HAND IMU acc_x acc_y acc_z gyr_x gyr_y gyr_z g ×3, dps ×3 imu_ring MudraPro-<device_id>-IMU_RING IMU same as imu_hand g / dps ppg_h MudraPro-<device_id>-PPG_H PPG ch0 ch1 (hand) microvolts ppg_f MudraPro-<device_id>-PPG_F PPG ch0 ch1 (finger/ring) microvolts On a Mudra Ultimate, names start with MudraUltimate- instead. imu_hand and imu_ring are what the rest of this SDK calls the hand IMU
( H_IMU ) and the finger IMU ( F_IMU ). The EMG and IMU stream names match
the Mudra Pro C++ SDK’s LSL streams, so a lab set up for one finds the
other’s streams unchanged. ppg_h and ppg_f are the hand ( PPG_H ) and finger/ring ( PPG_F ) PPG
sensors, two channels each. They share one chip, so both streams always
have the same sample rate. Sample rate ( nominal_srate ) is the sensor’s current ODR. Values are float32 , in the physical units the SDK already delivers
( data_format.md ) — the bridge doesn’t rescale anything. source_id is mudra_pro:<serial>:<sensor> ( mudra_ultimate:… on
Ultimate). It stays the same across restarts, which is how a recorder
reconnects to a stream that went away and came back. Stream description (the XML LabRecorder saves into the file):
manufacturer, model, device_id , serial, transport, and each channel’s
label, unit and type ( Accelerometer / Gyroscope for the IMU channels). bridge.streams maps each published sensor to its stream name. A sensor the device doesn’t answer for within status_timeout is skipped with a warning and listed in bridge.skipped — for example imu_ring on a
Mudra Pro, which has no finger IMU (finger IMU is Mudra Ultimate only), and ppg_f with no ring connected (the device answers its status query with an
error, just like the finger IMU’s). start() raises RuntimeError only if no requested sensor answers. 4. The bridge turns sensors on and off ¶ In this SDK, registering a sensor’s set_on_*_ready callback is what turns
the sensor on, and each sensor has exactly one callback slot
( SENSORS.md §1 ). So: start() turns on every sensor it publishes, by registering the
bridge’s own callback for it. Don’t turn them on yourself first. stop() turns them off. Nothing else does — not disconnect() , and not
your app exiting
( Turning sensors off is the app’s job ).
Call stop() before disconnecting, or use async with . Don’t register a published sensor’s callback yourself. It would replace
the bridge’s, and the stream would go silent. To also use the samples in
your own code (a live chart, a local recorder), read them back from LSL
with a pylsl.StreamInlet , like any other LSL consumer (§3). Sensors the bridge doesn’t publish are left alone — register your own
callbacks on those as usual. The bridge publishes each package right inside its callback: it reorders the
samples into rows (the SDK delivers them channel by channel), timestamps them,
and calls push_chunk . That only copies the data into liblsl’s send buffer,
so it doesn’t hold up the device connection. 5. Timestamps — how devices get aligned ¶ Every package the SDK delivers carries timestamp : the device’s clock reading
(1 MHz, counting from boot) for the package’s first sample
( data_format.md ). It is
precise — taken on the sensor when the data was sampled, before any radio or
USB delay — but it isn’t in the host’s clock. The bridge converts it with a DeviceClockMapper : r = arrival time - device time # per package: clock offset + transport delay offset = smallest r of the last 20 s # delay only adds, so the smallest r is closest to the truth sample i = device time + offset + i / ODR # the package's first sample, then 1/ODR apart What that gives you: Stamps follow the device’s own sample timing. BLE and USB deliver
packages in bursts, with delays that vary by tens of milliseconds; none of
that jitter reaches the timestamps. A small constant lag. Stamps are late by the smallest transport delay
seen (about one BLE connection interval or USB transfer). Every sensor of a
device shares one mapper, so the lag is the same for all of them and they
stay aligned with each other. Aligned with every other LSL device. Stamps are in LSL’s clock, so a
recorder lines Mudra data up with everything else. Across machines, LSL’s
own clock synchronization takes care of the rest. The first second after start() is not published. The first packages
arrive late, so the offset improves quickly at first; the bridge drops
packages until it has settled. After that, the offset only changes slowly
(at most 0.2 ms per second), so timestamps never jump backwards — EMG at
3200 Hz has only 0.3 ms between samples. After a reboot or reconnect, call start() again (§6). It resets the
clock conversion, so there’s another second of warm-up. 6. Changing configuration, and reconnecting ¶ Changing a sensor’s configuration. A sensor must be off while its ODR,
resolution, or channel count changes
( SENSORS.md §3 ),
and a stream’s sample rate and channel count are fixed when it’s created. So
stop the bridge, change the configuration, and start it again: async def change_emg_rate ( bridge , device ): await bridge . stop () # turns the sensors off # 800 Hz is a Mudra Pro rate; Mudra Ultimate's are 500/1000/2000/4000 Hz await device . set_emg_odr ( device . EMG_ODR_ENUM . from_value ( 800 )) await bridge . start () # new streams at the new rate start() asks the device for each sensor’s current status, so the new streams
always match the new configuration. The streams keep their source_id , so
LabRecorder picks them back up. If the channel count changes while the bridge is running anyway, packages stop
fitting the stream: the bridge logs a warning and drops them until you call start() again. After a disconnect. A disconnect clears every per-device callback
( CALLBACKS.md §3 ),
including the bridge’s, so the streams go silent. Once the device is
connected again — await device.connect() has returned and await Mudra().is_connected(device) is true — call await bridge.start() ;
it rebuilds the streams and turns the sensors back on. Calling start() on a running bridge is always safe: it stops it first, then
starts again. 7. Multiple devices ¶ Use one bridge per device, each with its own device_id (the default, the
device serial, already differs from band to band). Mudra supports several
connected devices at once
( CONNECTION.md §8 ): async def stream_both ( left , right ): async with MudraLslBridge ( left , "left" ), MudraLslBridge ( right , "right" ): await asyncio . sleep ( 3600 ) # MudraPro-left-EMG, MudraPro-right-EMG, ... 8. Troubleshooting ¶ ImportError from start() — pylsl isn’t installed, or on Linux, liblsl is missing. See §1. RuntimeError from start() — no sensor answered within status_timeout . Check that the connection succeeded and start the bridge
only after await device.connect() has returned (not from on_mudra_device_connected ); on a slow link, raise status_timeout . A sensor is missing from bridge.streams — the device didn’t report
that sensor’s status; bridge.skipped says so. A Mudra Pro (no finger IMU)
never reports imu_ring . A stream exists but carries no data — look for the bridge’s warning that
the device didn’t turn the sensor on. The device refused the “turn on”
command, often because the configuration exceeds its license tier: sign in
first ( AUTH.md ), and register set_on_command_error_received to
see the device’s reason. Also check that nothing else in your app registered
that sensor’s callback (§4). A “package … doesn’t fit N channels” warning — the channel count changed
while the bridge was running. Use stop → configure → start (§6). LabRecorder on another machine doesn’t see the streams — LSL finds
streams by UDP multicast and sends data over TCP; both must get through the
firewall, on the network interface that reaches the other machine. Try a
recorder on the same machine first. See troubleshooting.md . Related documentation ¶ Sensor streams and configuration: SENSORS.md · sample layout
and units: data_format.md · callbacks: CALLBACKS.md API reference: api_reference → “Lab Streaming Layer” Usage guide (package layout, architecture): SDK_USAGE.md

title: Mudra SDK — Usage Guide
text:
Mudra SDK — Usage Guide ¶ Kavana SDK is the Python SDK (package mudra_sdk ) for the Mudra Pro and Mudra Ultimate wearables. It supports two transports — BLE (Bluetooth
Low Energy) and CDC (the USB connection: the device’s USB CDC-ACM virtual
serial ports) — behind one unified, asyncio -based API. It is written to be usable both by humans and by other coding agents/bots
that need to integrate against this SDK. The snippets follow patterns taken
from the SDK itself and from the reference app, examples/connect_app.py (the launcher for the examples/mudra_connect package). §4 below is a complete script; snippets
elsewhere are excerpts that assume an already-connected device and omit
imports unless they’re shown. This guide is split into focused pages: Page Covers This page Package layout, setup, core architecture, a minimal end-to-end example CONNECTION.md Scanning, connecting/disconnecting over BLE and CDC, ping, licensing/account sign-in, raw/advanced commands, firmware update (DFU) AUTH.md Account sign-in and device licensing — read this before building an app , not just a script SENSORS.md Enabling/disabling sensor streams, querying/configuring status (ODR, resolution, ranges), packet-loss test mode, SD card recording CALLBACKS.md Every callback in the SDK — the global MudraDelegate and all per-device set_on_* callbacks — with signatures and firing conditions LSL.md Lab Streaming Layer integration — publishing a device’s sensors as LSL streams ( mudra_sdk.lsl.MudraLslBridge , examples/lsl_app.py ) 1. Package layout ¶ mudra_sdk/
  auth.py                 Account sign-in + license/user_id provisioning (see AUTH.md)
  models/
    mudra.py              Mudra — top-level singleton: scan/connect/disconnect, delegate dispatch
    mudra_device.py       MudraDevice — per-device API: sensors, streaming, storage
    mudra_pro.py          MudraPro — Mudra Pro subclass (3-ch EMG)
    mudra_ultimate.py     MudraUltimate — Mudra Ultimate subclass (8-ch EMG)
    cdc_device.py         CdcDevice — CDC device identity (address/ports)
    callbacks.py          MudraDelegate / BleServiceDelegate / CdcServiceDelegate ABCs
    enums.py              Pro/UltimateFirmwareCommand, SensorTypes, ODR/range enums, status/error codes
    license_manager.py    LicenseManager — renews a device's license before it expires (see AUTH.md)
    data_recorder.py      PC-side JSON recording (start_recording/get_json_recording)
    computation_wrapper.py Thin wrapper around the native MudraSDK library (parsing, packet loss)
    firmware_protocol.py  Binary CONFIG-frame builders used by the BLE transport
  service/
    ble_service.py        BLE transport (bleak) — scanning, GATT, notifications
    cdc_service.py         CDC transport (pyserial) — USB serial scanning, ASCII protocol
    dfu_service.py         Firmware update (MCUmgr/SMP over a third USB-CDC port) — USB only
  lsl/                    Optional Lab Streaming Layer publisher (MudraLslBridge) — see LSL.md
  libs/                   Native MudraSDK shared library (.dll/.so/.dylib), loaded via ctypes The main entry points: from mudra_sdk import Mudra , MudraDevice , MudraPro , MudraUltimate , MudraModel from mudra_sdk import auth # sign-in + provisioning (AUTH.md) from mudra_sdk.service import DfuError , DfuStage # firmware update (CONNECTION.md §6) FirmwareCallbacks and FirmwareDetails are also exported from the package
root, but they’re internal protocol/constant tables, not something an app
needs. 2. Setup ¶ There is no PyPI package / pip install yet — the SDK is used by adding the
repo root to sys.path , exactly as the example app does: import sys from pathlib import Path # Must be the folder that CONTAINS mudra_sdk/ (the repo root), not mudra_sdk/ itself. _REPO_ROOT = Path ( __file__ ) . resolve () . parent if str ( _REPO_ROOT ) not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , str ( _REPO_ROOT )) from mudra_sdk import Mudra , MudraDevice Requires Python 3.10+. Install the dependencies with pip install -r mudra_sdk/requirements.txt — bleak (BLE; installed from a
git fork, so git must be on your PATH ), pyserial (CDC), requests / urllib3 (cloud), and smpclient (firmware update over CDC — see CONNECTION.md §6 ). The native MudraSDK shared library under mudra_sdk/libs/<platform>/<arch>/ is loaded automatically and is required for any device work : it parses
sensor data and also supplies the BLE command bytes and CDC command tokens.
If it’s missing for your platform, Mudra() still constructs (with a logged
warning), but no MudraDevice can be created — each one raises RuntimeError("Native library is not loaded") — so scans find nothing. Only
the cloud calls ( mudra_sdk.auth , MudraServerClient ) work without it. Async vs. sync. Everything that talks to a device or transport is a
coroutine — scanning, connect() / disconnect() , every set_on_* setter,
and every get_* / set_* sensor command — so call it from inside an asyncio
event loop. The plain synchronous calls include the cached getters
( get_*_status_info() , get_license_device_info() , get_firmware_version_info() , the packet-loss getters), get_json_recording() , auth.sign_in_email() / auth.logout() / auth.get_user_ref() , and every MudraServerClient call. The cloud ones do blocking HTTP — from async code, run
them via await asyncio.to_thread(...) (or run_in_executor ). The example
app runs its own asyncio loop on a background thread (see examples/mudra_connect/async_bridge.py )
because it’s a Tkinter GUI; a plain script can just use asyncio.run(...) . Callbacks are plain functions. Delegate methods and per-device set_on_* callbacks are called directly (not awaited) on the asyncio loop thread — write
them with def , not async def (an async def callback never runs). Keep
them fast, and schedule any async follow-up with asyncio.create_task(...) . 3. Core architecture ¶ Mudra — a process-wide singleton. Owns both transports
( BleService , CdcService ) and dispatches every device event to your delegate. You never construct more than one; Mudra() always returns the
same instance. MudraDevice — one object per discovered device address, on either
transport (in practice a MudraPro or MudraUltimate subclass, picked from
the detected model). The same physical device seen over both BLE and USB is
two separate objects. Check device.transport ( "ble" or "cdc" ) if you
need to branch — most callers don’t need to, since every method already
branches internally and picks the right wire format. MudraDelegate — an abstract base class you implement to receive
connection lifecycle events and device-discovery events. Register it once
via Mudra().set_delegate(...) . See CALLBACKS.md . Per-device callbacks — sensor data, status replies, errors, etc. are
delivered per-device via await device.set_on_*(fn) setters,
not through the global delegate. See CALLBACKS.md . Mudra()  ── scan_ble()/scan_cdc() ──► MudraDelegate.on_device_discovered(device)
        │                                     │
        │                     await device.connect() (transport-aware)
        │                       (fires on_mudra_device_connected along the way)
        │                                     ▼
        │                       connect() returns → device ready
        │                                     │
        │                device.set_on_emg_ready(cb) / set_on_emg_status_received(cb) / ...
        ▼                                     ▼
   device.disconnect()              cb(...) fires as data/status arrives 4. Minimal end-to-end example ¶ import asyncio from mudra_sdk import Mudra from mudra_sdk.models.callbacks import MudraDelegate from mudra_sdk.models.mudra_device import MudraDevice class MyDelegate ( MudraDelegate ): def __init__ ( self ): self . found = asyncio . Event () self . device : MudraDevice | None = None def on_device_discovered ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( f "Found { device . name } ( { device . transport } ) @ { device . address } " ) self . device = device self . found . set () # All delegate methods are plain `def` — the SDK calls them without awaiting. def on_mudra_device_connected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "link open" ) def on_mudra_device_connecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "connecting..." ) def on_mudra_device_disconnecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "disconnecting..." ) def on_mudra_device_disconnected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "disconnected" ) def on_mudra_device_connection_failed ( self , device : MudraDevice , error : str ): print ( f "connect failed: { error } " ) def on_bluetooth_state_changed ( self , state : bool ): pass # required, but never fired async def main (): mudra = Mudra () delegate = MyDelegate () mudra . set_delegate ( delegate ) await mudra . scan_ble () await mudra . scan_cdc () await asyncio . wait_for ( delegate . found . wait (), timeout = 15 ) await mudra . stop_scan_ble () await mudra . stop_scan_cdc () device = delegate . device await device . connect () # returns once the SDK's connect sequence is done; never raises if not await mudra . is_connected ( device ): return # failure was reported via on_mudra_device_connection_failed def on_emg ( timestamp , samples , frequency , frequency_std ): print ( f "EMG @ { frequency } Hz: { len ( samples ) } samples" ) try : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( on_emg ) # enables the EMG sensor + starts streaming await asyncio . sleep ( 5 ) finally : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( None ) # turns it off again — disconnecting doesn't await device . disconnect () asyncio . run ( main ()) When is the device ready? When await device.connect() returns. By then
the SDK has finished its connect sequence — BLE: services discovered,
notifications subscribed, initial status/license/ user_id queries sent; CDC:
both ports opened and handshaken, initial status queries and provisioning
sent, then START . That’s the point to enable sensors. Over BLE the status replies arrive asynchronously afterwards (over CDC they’re read back before connect() returns) — register status callbacks before connect() if you
want them (see SENSORS.md §2 ). MudraDelegate.on_mudra_device_connected fires earlier , as soon as the
link is open and before that setup (BLE: before notifications are subscribed;
CDC: before the status queries and START ) — use it for UI state, not as the
signal to start sending commands. connect() never raises on failure: a
failure arrives via on_mudra_device_connection_failed , so check await mudra.is_connected(device) after it returns. For everything beyond this minimal example, see: CONNECTION.md · SENSORS.md · CALLBACKS.md 5. Quick reference — key enums ( mudra_sdk.models.enums ) ¶ Enum Values Used for SensorTypes EMG , H_IMU , F_IMU , PPG_H , PPG_F Mostly internal (status-reply routing); you rarely need it FirmwareDataType emg , imuH , imuF , ppgH , ppgF Mostly internal (which stream to power on/off); you enable streams via set_on_*_ready instead ProEMGODR 200/400/800/1600/2133/3200/4267/6400 (Hz) set/get_emg_odr on MudraPro UltimateEMGODR 500/1000/2000/4000 (Hz) set/get_emg_odr on MudraUltimate EmgRes 16, 24 (bits) set/get_emg_res IMUODR 25/50/100/200/400/800/1600 (Hz) set/get_{h,f}_imu_odr IMUAccRange 2/4/8/16 (g) Reported in ImuStatus.accel_range_g . set_{h,f}_imu_acc takes the plain int (e.g. 4 ), not the enum member IMUGyrRange 125/250/500/1000/2000 (dps) Reported in ImuStatus.gyro_range_dps . set_{h,f}_imu_gyr takes the plain int (e.g. 500 ), not the enum member PPGODR 25/50/100/200/400 (Hz) set/get_ppg_h_odr / set/get_ppg_f_odr (one chip-wide value) BtCmdId SYSTEM , EMG , H_IMU , F_IMU , PPG_H , BAT , LED , BT_CTRL , TAP , STORAGE , PPG_F Identifying which subsystem a command-error is about BtCmdStatus OK , ERR_UNKNOWN , ERR_INVALID , ERR_BUSY , ERR_STATE , ERR_HARDWARE , ERR_INTERNAL , ERR_BT_NOT_READY , ERR_LICENSE , ERR_BLE_RATE , ERR_FILE_EXISTS , ERR_SD_WRITE Error codes on any failed command Every enum in this table has .value_int and a static .from_value(int) (returns None for an unknown value) — not every enum in the module does; BtCmdId / BtCmdStatus also have .description (human-readable name) — use that rather than the raw .value for anything user-facing or logged.

title: Mudra SDK — Sensors Guide (Enable / Disable / Status / Config)
text:
Mudra SDK — Sensors Guide (Enable / Disable / Status / Config) ¶ Part of the Mudra SDK usage guide . See also: CONNECTION.md · CALLBACKS.md Assumes the device is already connected — see CONNECTION.md . All examples below run on a connected device: MudraDevice . All callbacks on this page are plain def functions — the SDK calls them
directly without awaiting, so an async def callback never runs (see CALLBACKS.md ). The device has five sensors, each identified consistently across the API: Sensor Description FirmwareDataType SensorTypes EMG Electromyography emg EMG H_IMU Hand IMU (accel + gyro) imuH H_IMU F_IMU Finger IMU (accel + gyro) imuF F_IMU PPG_H Hand photoplethysmography (2 channels) ppgH PPG_H PPG_F Finger (ring) photoplethysmography (2 channels) ppgF PPG_F PPG_H and PPG_F are two sensors on one PPG chip, split the same way the
hand and finger IMUs are: PPG_H carries the band’s two optical channels,
PPG_F the ring’s two. Each has its own stream, status, enable/disable and
per-channel settings, but some settings belong to the chip and are shared —
see §3 . PPG_F needs the ring connected,
like F_IMU. There are two independent axes for each sensor — don’t conflate them: Streaming data ( set_on_<sensor>_ready ) — registering a callback is the enable/disable action; the sensor is powered on the wire the
moment you set a non- None callback, and powered off when you set None . There is no separate “enable” call. Status / configuration ( get_<sensor>_status , set_on_<sensor>_status_received ) — a point-in-time or pushed report of
whether the sensor is on, and at what ODR/resolution/range. Purely
informational; doesn’t turn anything on or off by itself. 1. Enable / disable a sensor’s data stream ¶ def on_emg_data ( timestamp : int , samples : list [ float ], frequency : int , frequency_std : float ): ... # samples is one decoded block of EMG values, already parsed by the native lib await device . set_on_emg_ready ( on_emg_data ) # ENABLE EMG — sends the firmware power-on command await device . set_on_emg_ready ( None ) # DISABLE EMG — sends power-off, drops the callback Same shape for the other four sensors: await device . set_on_imu_h_ready ( callback_or_none ) await device . set_on_imu_f_ready ( callback_or_none ) await device . set_on_ppg_h_ready ( callback_or_none ) await device . set_on_ppg_f_ready ( callback_or_none ) Callback signature for all five is identical: (timestamp: int, samples: list[float], frequency: int, frequency_std: float) -> None .
(Full callback catalog: CALLBACKS.md .)
Register these only after await device.connect() has returned — they send
the power command over the live connection. samples is channel-major (each channel’s full run back to back, not
interleaved per-sample), and frequency is the package rate, not the
sensor’s ODR — see data_format.md before writing any
parsing code against it. Internally, setting any of these callbacks recomputes “is this data type
needed” (native is_data_needed : a ready-callback is registered, or an
active PC-side recording — start_recording(...) , §6 — includes that
sensor) and only sends the firmware enable/disable command over BLE or the <SENSOR>_ON / <SENSOR>_OFF CDC token when that answer changes. So set_on_<sensor>_ready(None) powers the sensor off unless something else
in-process still needs it (e.g. a running start_recording ), in which case
it stays on until that stops too. You don’t send power commands directly. Each sensor has exactly one callback slot — a second set_on_<sensor>_ready call replaces the first, it doesn’t add a listener. If a MudraLslBridge is publishing a sensor, it already uses that slot:
registering your own callback would replace the bridge’s and silence its
stream — read the samples back from LSL instead
( LSL.md §4 ). Turning sensors off is the app’s job ¶ Enabling a sensor powers it on on the device , not just in your process.
It keeps running until your app disables it ( set_on_<sensor>_ready(None) )
or the device is powered off. Nothing else turns it off: device.disconnect() doesn’t turn sensors off. Over CDC it pauses the
data stream ( STOP ), but the sensors themselves stay on. Your app exiting or crashing doesn’t turn them off either. For example:
enable EMG, close the app without disabling it, and EMG keeps running on
the device, draining its battery with nobody reading the data. The next session to connect will find the sensor still on
( get_emg_status() reports enabled=True ). So disable every sensor you enabled before you disconnect or exit — in a finally block or shutdown handler, so it also runs on errors: try : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( on_emg_data ) ... # use the stream finally : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( None ) # turn off what you turned on await device . disconnect () If the connection drops unexpectedly (out of range, USB unplugged), the
power-off command can’t be sent — the sensor stays on until you reconnect
and disable it, or the device is powered off. Note that the SDK starts every
connection assuming all sensors are off, so after reconnecting, set_on_emg_ready(None) on its own sends nothing. To turn off a sensor left
running, toggle it: register a callback (sends power-on), then set None (sends power-off). 2. Query / observe sensor status ¶ One-shot query — fires the corresponding status callback (below) when
the reply arrives; it’s async/fire-and-forget, not a return value: await device . get_emg_status () await device . get_h_imu_status () await device . get_f_imu_status () await device . get_ppg_h_status () await device . get_ppg_f_status () Register a status callback to receive every status reply — both the
ones you triggered with a get_*_status() call and unsolicited pushes the
firmware sends after a config change: from mudra_sdk.models.mudra_device import EmgStatus , ImuStatus , PpgStatus def on_emg_status ( status : EmgStatus ): # plain def, not async def print ( status . enabled , status . odr_sps , status . resolution_bits ) await device . set_on_emg_status_received ( on_emg_status ) # on_h_imu_status / on_f_imu_status / on_ppg_h_status / on_ppg_f_status are # your own functions, same shape: await device . set_on_h_imu_status_received ( on_h_imu_status ) # receives ImuStatus await device . set_on_f_imu_status_received ( on_f_imu_status ) # receives ImuStatus await device . set_on_ppg_h_status_received ( on_ppg_h_status ) # receives PpgStatus await device . set_on_ppg_f_status_received ( on_ppg_f_status ) # receives PpgStatus Status dataclasses ( mudra_sdk.models.mudra_device ): @dataclass class EmgStatus : enabled : bool odr_sps : ProEMGODR # or UltimateEMGODR on MudraUltimate (different AFE, different rates) # e.g. ProEMGODR.emgOdr3200 -> .value_int == 3200 resolution_bits : EmgRes # EmgRes.emgRes16 / emgRes24 -> .bits @dataclass class ImuStatus : # shared by H_IMU and F_IMU enabled : bool odr_hz : IMUODR accel_range_g : IMUAccRange gyro_range_dps : IMUGyrRange @dataclass class PpgStatus : # shared by PPG_H and PPG_F enabled : bool # this sensor's own on/off state odr_hz : PPGODR # chip-wide: PPG_H and PPG_F always report the same ODR Cached last-known status (no round trip, may be None before the
first reply arrives): device . get_emg_status_info () -> Optional [ EmgStatus ] device . get_h_imu_status_info () -> Optional [ ImuStatus ] device . get_f_imu_status_info () -> Optional [ ImuStatus ] device . get_ppg_h_status_info () -> Optional [ PpgStatus ] device . get_ppg_f_status_info () -> Optional [ PpgStatus ] The SDK sends all five get_*_status() queries itself during connect() (BLE: once the COMMAND characteristic is discovered; CDC: from on_cdc_ready() ). Over BLE the replies arrive shortly after connect() returns; over CDC they’re read back before it returns. Either way get_*_status_info() is usually populated soon after. To see those first
replies in your status callback, register it before calling connect() (status callbacks don’t need a live connection, and stay
registered until the next disconnect) or from on_mudra_device_connected .
The streaming setters ( set_on_*_ready , §1) are different — call those only
after connect() returns. 3. Configure a sensor (ODR, resolution, ranges, etc.) ¶ Important — disable the sensor before changing its configuration. set_emg_odr / set_emg_res / set_h_imu_odr / set_ppg_h_odr /etc. just send the
config command over the wire — they do not check whether the sensor is
currently streaming, and the firmware does not stop it for you. If a
sensor is enabled when you send an ODR/resolution/range change, do it
yourself: was_enabled = device . get_emg_status_info () and device . get_emg_status_info () . enabled if was_enabled : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( None ) # 1. disable first await device . set_emg_odr ( ProEMGODR . emgOdr3200 ) # 2. change config if was_enabled : await device . set_on_emg_ready ( on_emg_data ) # 3. re-enable Same pattern for H_IMU/F_IMU/PPG_H/PPG_F — for PPG, disable both PPG
sensors first (see below). Skipping the disable step risks a
rejected command, a corrupted/mismatched data stream, or firmware-side
undefined behavior depending on sensor and transport. Every config parameter follows the same set_x / get_x pair, and both
return None . Replies to the individual parameter GETs ( get_emg_odr() , get_h_imu_acc() , get_ppg_h_dec() , …) currently reach no callback — they
only show up in the SDK’s debug log. To read the current configuration, call get_<sensor>_status() and use the status callback or the cached get_<sensor>_status_info() (§2), which report ODR, resolution and ranges.
A rejected SET or GET still arrives via the command-error callback (below). from mudra_sdk.models.enums import ProEMGODR , EmgRes , IMUODR , PPGODR # On a MudraUltimate, use UltimateEMGODR instead — different AFE (ADS1298 vs # Pro's ADS1293), different discrete rate set (500/1000/2000/4000 Hz). await device . set_emg_odr ( ProEMGODR . emgOdr3200 ) # samples/sec await device . get_emg_odr () await device . set_emg_res ( EmgRes . emgRes24 ) # bit depth await device . get_emg_res () await device . get_emg_res_max () # read-only, max post-process value await device . set_h_imu_odr ( IMUODR . imuHOdr200 ) await device . set_h_imu_acc ( 4 ) # accel range, g — IMUAccRange values: 2/4/8/16 await device . set_h_imu_gyr ( 500 ) # gyro range, dps — IMUGyrRange: 125/250/500/1000/2000 await device . set_h_imu_acc_bw ( 2 ) # bandwidth divisor await device . set_h_imu_acc_avg ( 4 ) # averaging samples # ...get_h_imu_* mirrors each set_h_imu_*; f_imu_* is identical, just for the finger IMU await device . set_ppg_h_odr ( PPGODR . ppgOdr100 ) # chip-wide: PPG_F follows await device . set_ppg_h_dec ( 4 ) # decimation factor, chip-wide await device . set_ppg_h_prpct ( 1280 ) # pulse-repetition period code, chip-wide await device . set_ppg_h_led ( ch = 0 , drv1 = 10 , drv2 = 10 ) await device . set_ppg_h_tia ( ch = 0 , rf = 1 , cf = 1 ) await device . set_ppg_h_src ( ch = 0 , led = 1 , pd = 1 ) await device . ppg_h_clear () # ...set_ppg_f_* / get_ppg_f_* / ppg_f_clear are identical, for the ring's channels PPG_H and PPG_F share one chip ¶ ODR, decimation ( dec ) and PRPCT are chip-wide. Setting one through
either sensor ( set_ppg_h_odr or set_ppg_f_odr ) changes it for both,
and both sensors’ status reports the new ODR. LED, TIA and SRC are per channel and take the sensor’s own channel
number, ch=0 or ch=1 , on both sensors — not the chip’s 0–3. Anything
else raises ValueError before anything is sent. ppg_h_clear() / ppg_f_clear() drop that sensor’s two channels’
LED/TIA/SRC overrides, plus the shared PRPCT override. Config changes are rejected while either PPG sensor is streaming —
disable both before changing any PPG setting, on either sensor. PPG_F needs the ring. Without it, enabling PPG_F or changing a PPG_F
per-channel setting is rejected with BtCmdStatus.ERR_STATE (via the
command-error callback below), and so is get_ppg_f_status() — no PpgStatus arrives. That is exactly how F_IMU reports a missing ring (the
device checks the same ring for both). If the ring is unplugged while PPG_F
is on, PPG_F stays enabled but its callback stops firing until the ring is
back. Errors on any of the above (a rejected SET, an invalid value, etc.)
arrive via one callback regardless of which sensor or transport: from mudra_sdk.models.enums import BtCmdId , BtCmdStatus def on_command_error ( cmd_id : BtCmdId , status : BtCmdStatus ): # plain def print ( f " { cmd_id . description } failed: { status . description } (0x { status . value_int : 02X } )" ) await device . set_on_command_error_received ( on_command_error ) Over CDC, the firmware itself rejects a config change on a running sensor;
that arrives here as BtCmdStatus.ERR_BUSY (see CALLBACKS.md §2.4 for how CDC error replies map to
status codes). 4. Packet-loss test mode ¶ Both models. A firmware-side overlay, per sensor, that replaces one channel
with an incrementing counter so loss can be measured without inspecting real
data. On Mudra Ultimate it needs firmware newer than 1.0.3.8, which doesn’t
have these commands and rejects them: await device . set_emg_test_mode ( True ) # also: set_h_imu_test_mode / set_f_imu_test_mode / #       set_ppg_h_test_mode / set_ppg_f_test_mode seen , lost = device . get_emg_packet_loss_stats () # lifetime counters (also *_h_imu_*, *_ppg_h_*, ...) pct = device . sample_emg_packet_loss () # windowed (~1s) loss %, call periodically hz = device . get_emg_packet_loss_rate_hz () device . reset_emg_packet_loss_window () await device . set_emg_test_mode ( False ) # turn it off again Test mode is one combined firmware command on both BLE and CDC: turning it
on also starts the sensor, and set_emg_test_mode(False) stops the sensor
again. 5. SD card recording ( BLE only ) ¶ Starts/stops the device’s own on-board recording to a /SD:/REC_<n>/ session folder of size-capped binary part files, MREC -tagged, not CSV. Not available over CDC — every call below on a CDC
device immediately reports BtCmdStatus.ERR_UNKNOWN via the command-error
callback instead of sending anything. Requires the device’s PRO license tier — on FREE/PLUS a start is
rejected with BtCmdStatus.ERR_LICENSE (via the command-error callback)
without touching any sensor. See §5 of CONNECTION.md for provisioning a tier. The device needs a 16-byte user_id before it will start a recording. If
you were signed in when the device connected, the SDK already sent it (see AUTH.md ); otherwise call set_user_id(...) yourself with exactly 16 bytes: import time # Register callbacks first, so no reply is missed. await device . set_on_storage_record_state_received ( lambda status : ... ) # RecordStatus await device . set_on_storage_record_error_received ( lambda status : ... ) # BtCmdStatus await device . set_on_storage_next_file_num_received ( lambda file_num : ... ) # int await device . get_storage_record_state () # -> RecordStatus via callback await device . get_storage_next_file_num () # -> int via callback # Only needed if the SDK didn't already send it at connect (signed out): await device . set_user_id ( user_id ) # `user_id`: bytes, exactly 16 (else ValueError) await device . set_storage_record ( emg = True , ppg_h = False , imu_h = True , imu_f = False , ppg_f = False , file_num = 3 , duration_min = 0 , utc_ts = int ( time . time ()), description = "session notes" , is_test = False , ) The five sensor flags may be passed positionally, in this order ( emg , ppg_h , imu_h , imu_f , ppg_f ); everything after them is keyword-only,
and a flag that isn’t a bool (or 0/1) raises TypeError . duration_min (default 0) records until an explicit stop call; any other
value (1-65535) arms a one-shot firmware timer that automatically stops the
session after that many minutes — indistinguishable from calling set_storage_record(False, False, False, False, False, file_num=file_num) yourself: same
sensor teardown, same BT_STORAGE_RECORD_STATE push with active=False via
the state callback above. Ignored when stopping. An earlier stop (manual,
disconnect, or a write-failure abort) cancels the pending timer — nothing
renews it mid-session. utc_ts (default 0 = not supplied) is your wall-clock time in Unix epoch
seconds at session start (e.g. int(time.time()) ) — the device has no
independent RTC, so this is the only source of a real-world timestamp. When
non-zero, the firmware writes it into the recording’s second (auto-generated
summary) text line as UTC=<ts> , ahead of the sensor/ODR summary, and uses
it for nothing else — it does not set the device’s trusted clock (that’s apply_license() ’s job, via the token’s issued_at ; see CONNECTION.md §5 ). Ignored
when stopping. set_storage_record() fails with BtCmdStatus.ERR_STATE (via the
command-error callback) if set_user_id was never called. is_test=True arms packet-loss test mode on each newly-started sensor
before recording begins, so the recording captures the counter stream
instead of real data — inspect the counter
channel for gaps, for offline packet-loss analysis with no live link needed. Unlike storage/SD commands, set_user_id also works over CDC ( USER_ID <hex> ). 6. Sensor pitfalls ¶ Changing config on a live sensor — set_*_odr / set_*_res /range calls
don’t disable the sensor for you; see §3 above. Disable
( set_on_*_ready(None) ), change config, then re-enable if it was running. Expecting a return value from a get_* / set_* call — they all
return None . Status, storage and device-info replies come back
asynchronously through a registered callback (register it before triggering the request so you don’t miss it); replies to individual
parameter GETs ( get_emg_odr() , get_h_imu_acc() , …) reach no callback at
all — read config from the status callback / get_*_status_info() instead
(§3). Writing callbacks as async def — the SDK calls callbacks without
awaiting them, so an async def callback never runs. Use plain def . Forgetting None disables streaming — set_on_emg_ready(None) (and
the IMU/PPG equivalents) is the disable call, not just “clear my
callback”; it actually sends the power-off command (unless an active start_recording still needs that sensor). Leaving a sensor on when the app closes — neither disconnect() nor
exiting the app turns sensors off; they keep running until you disable
them or the device is powered off. See Turning sensors off is the app’s job . SD recording is BLE-only — see §5 above. Treating PPG settings as per-sensor — ODR, decimation and PRPCT are
shared by PPG_H and PPG_F, and PPG channel numbers are each sensor’s own
0–1 (PPG_F’s ch=0 is the ring’s first channel). See §3 .

device reboots and swaps to it right after — reconnect afterward to

channel 0 with an incrementing counter AND starts EMG
