title: Data format
text:
Data format ¶ What’s actually inside the samples: list[float] argument delivered to set_on_emg_ready / set_on_imu_h_ready / set_on_imu_f_ready / set_on_ppg_h_ready / set_on_ppg_f_ready callbacks ( SENSORS.md §1 ) —
sourced directly from the native parser
( mudra_sdk/core/Computation/CommonTypes.h , computation_wrapper.cpp ). samples is channel-major, not interleaved ¶ Each callback fires once per decoded package — one sensor’s section of the
DATA stream ( [id][len][payload][timestamp] , the same framing on BLE and
USB-CDC). The native parser buffers incoming bytes, so a single BLE
notification or CDC read may hold several sections or only part of one; you
get one callback per complete section. Each call carries every channel’s
samples from that package back to back — channel 0’s whole run, then channel 1’s whole run, and so on. It is not interleaved per-sample ( ch0, ch1, ch2, ch0, ch1, ch2, ... ). samples = [ ch0_s0 , ch0_s1 , ... , ch0_sN - 1 , # channel 0's samples ch1_s0 , ch1_s1 , ... , ch1_sN - 1 , # channel 1's samples ... ] len(samples) is always a multiple of the channel count for that sensor —
divide evenly to recover each channel’s run: def split_channels ( samples : list [ float ], channel_count : int ) -> list [ list [ float ]]: n = len ( samples ) // channel_count return [ samples [ ch * n :( ch + 1 ) * n ] for ch in range ( channel_count )] Channel count and order per sensor ¶ Sensor Channel count Order EMG 3 (Mudra Pro) / 8 (Mudra Ultimate) — device.EMG_CHANNEL_COUNT ch0, ch1, ..., chN-1 Hand IMU / Finger IMU Always 6 ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz (accel then gyro) Hand PPG / Finger PPG Always 2 ch0, ch1 — each sensor’s own channels (PPG_F’s are the ring’s two channels) Units — already scaled, not raw ADC counts ¶ The native parser scales every sample before it reaches the callback — you
never see raw ADC/register counts: EMG — scaled to ~[-1, 1] : raw count ÷ the active resolution’s
full-scale value (32767 at 16-bit, 4194304 = 0x400000 at 24-bit — the
same value get_emg_res_max() reports, see SENSORS.md §3 ). IMU (hand + finger) — accelerometer channels in g , gyroscope
channels in dps : raw ÷ 32768 × the currently configured accel/gyro
range ( IMUAccRange / IMUGyrRange — see ImuStatus ). Since range is
runtime-configurable, read it back rather than assuming the boot default. PPG (hand + finger) — scaled to microvolts (µV) via a fixed
AFE4950 count→µV factor (1.2 V / 2²¹ per count). Timestamp, frequency, and frequency_std ¶ The other three callback arguments, per package (not per individual sample): timestamp — the device clock reading for the package’s first sample ( ts_cyc , GRTC-backed, 64-bit, no rollover), in 1 MHz ticks (one tick per microsecond — mudra_sdk.lsl.GRTC_CPS ). Measured on Mudra Pro
fw 2.0.2.0 and Mudra Ultimate fw 1.0.3.0: where package sizes vary,
consecutive stamps differ by the previous package’s sample count × the
sample period. A device clock value, not a
host wall-clock time — don’t compare it directly against time.time() / time.perf_counter() . frequency — packages per second observed over roughly the last
1 second. This is not the sensor’s configured ODR ( ProEMGODR / IMUODR / PPGODR ) — one package typically bundles multiple
samples per channel, so package rate and per-channel sample rate are
different numbers. Read the actual ODR from the sensor’s status callback
( SENSORS.md §2 ) instead. frequency_std — standard deviation of that recent package-rate
history; a rough jitter indicator, not a per-sample error bound. See also ¶ SENSORS.md — enabling streams, status/config, packet-loss test mode. supported_devices.md — per-model channel counts and config ranges.

title: Examples
text:
Examples ¶ Two runnable apps live under examples/ , both built entirely on the public mudra_sdk API, never by touching BLE/serial wire formats directly: Mudra Connect ( examples/connect_app.py ,
the examples/mudra_connect package) — a Tkinter GUI covering scan,
connect, sensors, recording and auth, for any number of devices at once. Most snippets in the usage guide and its sub-pages follow patterns from it. LSL streamer ( examples/lsl_app.py , the examples/mudra_lsl package) — a headless command-line app that publishes
a device’s sensors to Lab Streaming Layer. Both launchers put the repo root on sys.path themselves, so run them from
anywhere with python examples/<app>.py . Install their dependencies with pip install -r examples/requirements.txt (the SDK’s own requirements plus matplotlib and pylsl ). The GUI needs Tkinter, which ships with the python.org installers on
Windows/macOS; on Linux install it from your distro (e.g. python3-tk ). It
runs its own asyncio event loop on a background thread
( examples/mudra_connect/async_bridge.py )
since Tkinter isn’t async-native. Mudra Connect The full reference app — scan, connect, live sensor charts, config, packet-loss, SD recording, firmware update, auth. LSL streamer Headless command-line app — find a device, connect, and publish its sensors as Lab Streaming Layer streams. Mudra Connect ¶ pip install - r examples / requirements . txt python examples / connect_app . py The primary reference app — examples/connect_app.py launches the examples/mudra_connect package, whose files are listed below
(paths relative to that package). The main window holds the scan buttons,
the sign-in bar and the device list. Connect as many devices as you like:
each connected device opens its own window with the tabs below, which only
ever talk to that device. Closing a device’s window disconnects it, and
clicking a connected device’s card brings its window to the front. Every
panel maps to one guide page: Panel Source Covers Devices devices.py BLE/CDC scan toggles, connect/disconnect — CONNECTION.md §1–2 Device windows device_window.py , state.py One window per connected device, each with its own state ( DeviceState ) — CONNECTION.md §8 Sensor charts charts.py , sensors.py Live EMG/IMU/PPG_H/PPG_F plots, per-sensor enable — SENSORS.md §1 Config panels/config.py ODR/resolution/range get/set per sensor — SENSORS.md §3 Packet loss panels/packet_loss.py , packet_loss_chart.py Test-mode toggle + live loss chart — SENSORS.md §4 Recording panels/recording.py (SD) / panels/pc_recording.py (host-side JSON) SD-card recording — SENSORS.md §5 Ping panels/ping.py , ping_chart.py Round-trip latency — CONNECTION.md §3 Command panels/command.py Raw/advanced commands, branching on device.transport — CONNECTION.md §4 Auth panels/auth.py Sign-in bar — AUTH.md Device indicators status_ui.py Each device window’s FW / battery / license-tier readouts, plus every status callback the app registers — CALLBACKS.md Firmware update panels/dfu.py DFU over USB-CDC — CONNECTION.md §6 The window looks the same on Windows, macOS and Linux: theme.py picks an
installed UI font and sizes text and spacing from the display’s scale
(including Linux desktop scaling, which Tk doesn’t detect on its own), and
side columns start at the width their content needs — drag a column’s edge
to resize it. If the detected scale looks wrong, override it, e.g. MUDRA_UI_SCALE=1.5 python examples/connect_app.py . delegate.py is the reference MudraDelegate implementation — it opens
and closes the device windows from the connection callbacks — and a good
template for your own ( CALLBACKS.md §1 ). Headless: stream to Lab Streaming Layer ¶ Not a GUI, but the second runnable entry point — python examples/lsl_app.py (a launcher over the examples/mudra_lsl/ package, same shape as the app
above) finds a device, connects, and publishes its sensors as LSL streams until
stopped, so LabRecorder or any pylsl consumer can record them time-aligned
with other instruments: pip install - r examples / requirements . txt # includes pylsl python examples / lsl_app . py -- name 48 - 25 -- sensors emg imu_hand -- duration 60 See LSL.md for the options and for the library API
( MudraLslBridge ) behind it.

title: FAQ
text:
FAQ ¶ Do I need an account to use the SDK? ¶ No. Connecting to a device never requires an account — a signed-out app
connects and streams fine, at whatever license tier the device already
holds. Signing in ( mudra_sdk.auth ) is what lets you raise that tier; see AUTH.md . Why do BLE and CDC behave slightly differently? ¶ They’re genuinely different links with different setup steps: BLE needs its
GATT services discovered and notifications subscribed, while CDC’s DATA port
stays silent until the SDK queries sensor status and explicitly sends START . The SDK does both inside connect() and hides most of the rest — every typed method already branches
internally — but a few things are transport-specific by nature: SD-card
recording and the PING firmware token are BLE-only; raw commands are binary
frames on BLE vs. ASCII lines on CDC. See CONNECTION.md . What does device.connect() returning tell me? ¶ That the SDK’s connect sequence has finished and you can enable sensors — if the connection succeeded. connect() returns only after its setup
(BLE: services discovered, notifications subscribed, initial status/license
queries sent; CDC: both ports open and handshaken, initial status queries
sent, then START ). It never raises on failure: the reason goes to MudraDelegate.on_mudra_device_connection_failed , so check await Mudra().is_connected(device) afterwards. MudraDelegate.on_mudra_device_connected fires earlier — as soon as the
link opens, before that setup — so use it for UI state, not for enabling
sensors. Status replies arrive asynchronously after connect() returns. See SDK_USAGE.md §4 . Why does setting a callback also enable the sensor? ¶ It’s a deliberate design choice, not a side effect to work around: for the
five sensor streams, “I want this data” and “the sensor should be powered
on” are the same fact, so there’s exactly one call
( set_on_<sensor>_ready(fn) / set_on_<sensor>_ready(None) ) instead of a
separate enable/disable pair plus a separate callback registration. See SENSORS.md §1 . Why does SD-card recording require the PRO tier? ¶ That’s a device-side policy enforced by firmware
( BtCmdStatus.ERR_LICENSE on FREE / PLUS ), not an SDK limitation — the SDK
just surfaces whatever the firmware decides. See supported_devices.md . Can I use this SDK without the native library? ¶ Only for cloud calls. Mudra() itself constructs with a log warning if the
native MudraSDK library is missing for your platform, but every MudraDevice raises RuntimeError("Native library is not loaded") when it’s
created — so scans find nothing and no device can be connected. The library
also supplies command encoding, sensor-data parsing, packet-loss statistics
and get_json_recording() . Without it, only mudra_sdk.auth and the cloud
client work. See native_library.md . Can I record Mudra data with LabRecorder / alongside an EEG system? ¶ Yes — mudra_sdk.lsl publishes each sensor as a Lab Streaming Layer stream,
timestamped from the device’s own clock, so LabRecorder (or any LSL consumer)
records it time-aligned with everything else on the network. It takes one
line of code ( async with MudraLslBridge(device): ... ), or none at all
( python examples/lsl_app.py ). pylsl is an optional extra. See LSL.md . Is there a PyPI package? ¶ Not yet — add the repo root to sys.path and import mudra_sdk directly.
See installation.md .

title: Quickstart
text:
Quickstart ¶ One API, two transports: scan over BLE , over USB-CDC , or both at
once — the same Mudra / MudraDevice calls work either way. import asyncio from mudra_sdk import Mudra from mudra_sdk.models.callbacks import MudraDelegate from mudra_sdk.models.mudra_device import MudraDevice class MyDelegate ( MudraDelegate ): def __init__ ( self ): self . found = asyncio . Event () self . device : MudraDevice | None = None def on_device_discovered ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( f "Found { device . name } ( { device . transport } ) @ { device . address } " ) self . device = device self . found . set () def on_mudra_device_connected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "connected" ) def on_mudra_device_connecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "connecting..." ) def on_mudra_device_disconnecting ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "disconnecting..." ) def on_mudra_device_disconnected ( self , device : MudraDevice ): print ( "disconnected" ) def on_mudra_device_connection_failed ( self , device : MudraDevice , error : str ): print ( f "connect failed: { error } " ) def on_bluetooth_state_changed ( self , state : bool ): print ( f "BT on= { state } " ) async def main (): mudra = Mudra () delegate = MyDelegate () mudra . set_delegate ( delegate ) await mudra . scan_ble () await mudra . scan_cdc () await asyncio . wait_for ( delegate . found . wait (), timeout = 15 ) await mudra . stop_scan_ble () await mudra . stop_scan_cdc () device = delegate . device await device . connect () # returns after the SDK's connect sequence; never raises if not await mudra . is_connected ( device ): return # the reason went to on_mudra_device_connection_failed def on_emg ( timestamp , samples , frequency , frequency_std ): print ( f "EMG @ { frequency } Hz: { len ( samples ) } samples" ) await device . set_on_emg_ready ( on_emg ) # enables the EMG sensor + starts streaming await asyncio . sleep ( 5 ) await device . set_on_emg_ready ( None ) # disables it again await device . disconnect () asyncio . run ( main ()) A few things worth knowing before you build on this: Setting a sensor callback is the enable/disable action — there’s no
separate “power on” call. set_on_emg_ready(fn) enables EMG and starts
delivering samples to fn ; set_on_emg_ready(None) disables it. Same
shape for set_on_imu_h_ready / set_on_imu_f_ready / set_on_ppg_h_ready / set_on_ppg_f_ready .
See SENSORS.md . await device.connect() returning is the “ready to enable sensors”
point. It returns only after the SDK’s connect sequence has finished (BLE:
services discovered and notifications subscribed; CDC: both ports open, the
initial status queries sent and START sent by the SDK). It never raises on
failure — the reason goes to on_mudra_device_connection_failed , so check await Mudra().is_connected(device) afterwards. on_mudra_device_connected fires earlier , as soon as the link opens and before that setup, so don’t
enable sensors from it. Status replies arrive asynchronously after connect() returns. See SDK_USAGE.md §4 . Connecting never requires an account. The device streams at whatever
license tier it already holds. See AUTH.md before shipping an
app that’s meant to unlock PLUS / PRO features. Next ¶ Usage guide — package layout, the Mudra / MudraDevice / MudraDelegate architecture. Connection guide — scanning, connect/disconnect, ping, raw commands, firmware update. Sensors guide — enabling streams, status/config, packet-loss test mode, SD recording. Callbacks reference — every callback in the SDK. Lab Streaming Layer guide — publish a device’s sensors to LSL for LabRecorder and other consumers. Examples — two full runnable reference apps.

title: Kavana SDK
text:
Kavana SDK ¶ Kavana SDK (Python package mudra_sdk ) is the Python SDK for the Mudra Pro and Mudra Ultimate wrist-worn sensor devices by Wearable
Devices. It presents one unified, asyncio -based API over two physically
different transports — BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) and USB-CDC (serial) — for the sensor streams (EMG, hand IMU, hand and finger PPG, plus a
finger IMU on Mudra Ultimate only), SD-card recording, firmware update, and account
sign-in/device licensing. The SDK is built for two audiences: External developers building applications and research workflows on top
of Mudra Pro / Mudra Ultimate. AI coding agents integrating the SDK on a developer’s behalf — every
guide page doubles as a reference an agent can integrate against directly. How the pieces fit ¶ Connecting to a device never requires an account — a signed-out app

every device event out to one registered delegate; MudraDevice is
transport-agnostic from the caller’s side ( Mudra SDK — Usage Guide ). BLE and CDC differ in setup, not in API shape — CDC needs a START before data flows, which the SDK sends for you inside connect() ; every
typed method already branches internally so callers rarely need to check device.transport themselves ( Mudra SDK — Connection Guide (Scan, BLE, CDC) ). title: Installation
text:
Installation ¶ There is no PyPI package yet. The SDK is used by adding the repo root to sys.path and importing mudra_sdk directly — exactly what the reference
apps under examples/ do: import sys from pathlib import Path _REPO_ROOT = Path ( __file__ ) . resolve () . parent # the folder that contains mudra_sdk/ if str ( _REPO_ROOT ) not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , str ( _REPO_ROOT )) from mudra_sdk import Mudra , MudraDevice Requirements: Python 3.10+ (the codebase uses dict[str, ...] -style
builtin generics and X | None unions) — 64-bit Python on Windows (see The native library below). git must be on your PATH , because bleak installs from a git URL. Everything the SDK needs is
pinned in mudra_sdk/requirements.txt : pip install -r mudra_sdk/requirements.txt What that installs, and why: bleak (the wearable-devices fork , develop branch) — the BLE transport. pyserial — the USB-CDC transport (scanning, opening CONFIG / DATA ports). requests / urllib3 — the cloud client behind mudra_sdk.auth (sign-in, license token fetch). smpclient — firmware update (DFU) over USB-CDC via MCUmgr/SMP. Your device also needs the firmware this SDK release supports: This SDK version ( 0.5.1 ) supports Mudra Pro firmware 2.0.2.6 and Mudra Ultimate firmware 1.0.3.9 . See Firmware compatibility . If you’re also running the example apps, install their extra
dependencies too (this pulls in mudra_sdk/requirements.txt transitively): pip install -r examples/requirements.txt # adds matplotlib and pylsl On Linux: BLE goes through BlueZ (the Bluetooth service must be running),
and opening the USB-CDC serial ports usually requires your user to be in the dialout group (or equivalent udev rule). To publish sensor streams onto the Lab Streaming Layer ( mudra_sdk.lsl , LSL.md ), install the optional pylsl dependency — nothing else in
the SDK needs it: pip install pylsl # liblsl ships in the Windows/macOS wheels; examples/requirements.txt includes it The native library ¶ mudra_sdk/core/ is a C++ project that builds MudraSDK.{dll,so,dylib} into mudra_sdk/libs/<platform>/<arch>/ . Prebuilt binaries for
windows-x64/macos-arm64/macos-x86_64/linux-x86_64/linux-aarch64 are checked
into the repo — rebuilt by CI whenever mudra_sdk/core/** changes —
so you never need a C++ toolchain just to use the SDK. On Windows only the x64 binary is current, so use 64-bit Python; the windows/x86 binary in
the tree is stale and unsupported. See native_library.md if you need to build it yourself. Mudra() loads this library lazily on first construction
( mudra_sdk/libs/library_loader.py , via ctypes ). The library is required
for any device work. If it’s missing for your platform, Mudra() still
constructs (it logs a warning instead of raising), but every MudraDevice raises RuntimeError("Native library is not loaded") when it’s created — so
scans find nothing and nothing can connect. The library also supplies
command encoding, sensor-data parsing, packet-loss stats and get_json_recording() . Only cloud calls ( mudra_sdk.auth and the cloud
client) work without it. Mostly async ¶ Device and transport calls — scanning, connect() / disconnect() , the set_on_* callback setters, and the get_* / set_* sensor commands — are
coroutines; call them from inside an asyncio event loop. A few calls are
plain synchronous functions: cached getters such as get_*_status_info() , get_license_device_info() , get_firmware_version_info() , and get_json_recording() ; mudra_sdk.auth.sign_in_email() / logout() / get_user_ref() ; every MudraServerClient call — these do blocking HTTP, so from async code run
them via asyncio.to_thread(...) (or loop.run_in_executor ). Callbacks you register are plain functions too (use def , not async def ). A plain script can just use asyncio.run(...) ; a GUI app that isn’t
async-native (like the Tkinter connect app under examples/ ) needs to run
its own event loop on a background thread — see examples/mudra_connect/async_bridge.py for that pattern. Next ¶ Quickstart — scan, connect, and stream in a dozen lines. Usage guide — package layout and core architecture. Supported devices — Mudra Pro vs. Mudra Ultimate.

title: Native library
text:
Native library ¶ mudra_sdk/core/ is a C++ CMake project that builds MudraSDK.{dll,so,dylib} — the native library that parses raw sensor byte streams (BLE notifications /
CDC serial reads) into timestamped per-sensor sample buffers and tracks
packet-loss statistics. mudra_sdk/libs/library_loader.py loads it via ctypes at runtime, from mudra_sdk/libs/<platform>/<arch>/ . What needs it ¶ The library is required for any device work . Mudra() loads it lazily,
inside __init__ , and only logs a warning if it’s missing or fails to load: # mudra_sdk/models/mudra.py try : self . _native_lib = load_library ( 'MudraSDK' , 'MudraSDK' ) except ( FileNotFoundError , OSError ) as e : logger . warning ( f "Could not load native library: { e } " ) self . _native_lib = None But every MudraDevice creates a ComputationWrapper around it, which raises RuntimeError("Native library is not loaded") when the library is absent —
so no device object can be created, and scans find nothing. Besides parsing
sensor data and tracking packet loss, the library also holds the per-model
command tables (the BLE command bytes and USB-CDC command tokens), and backs
the PC-side recording and get_json_recording() . Without it, only the cloud side works: mudra_sdk.auth sign-in and the
cloud client. CI builds and commits the binaries ¶ You almost never need to build this yourself — prebuilt binaries for every
supported platform/arch are checked into the repo under mudra_sdk/libs/ ,
rebuilt and re-committed by the maintainers’ CI whenever mudra_sdk/core/** changes, across: windows-x64 (64-bit Python only — the windows/x86 binary in the tree is
stale and unsupported) macos-arm64, macos-x86_64 ( mudra_sdk/libs/darwin/... ) linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64 If you do change anything under mudra_sdk/core/ , don’t hand-edit the .dll / .so / .dylib files — build locally instead. Note that a local
build writes straight into mudra_sdk/libs/<platform>/<arch>/ , overwriting
the checked-in binary for your platform: cmake -S mudra_sdk/core -B mudra_sdk/core/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Release
cmake --build mudra_sdk/core/build --config Release --parallel See mudra_sdk/core/CMakeLists.txt for
the exact output layout library_loader.py expects.

title: Supported devices
text:
Supported devices ¶ The SDK supports two hardware models, both exposed as a shared MudraDevice API with a small set of model-specific extras: Mudra Pro ( MudraPro ) — 3-channel EMG (ADS1293 AFE). Mudra Ultimate ( MudraUltimate ) — 8-channel EMG (ADS1298 AFE). Every method common to both — connect/disconnect, sensor enable/disable,
status, config, licensing, recording — is defined once on the shared MudraDevice base ( mudra_sdk/models/mudra_device.py ) and works identically
on either model. MudraPro / MudraUltimate ( mudra_sdk/models/mudra_pro.py , mudra_sdk/models/mudra_ultimate.py ) only add what differs. Model detection ¶ You never construct MudraPro / MudraUltimate directly — the SDK detects
the model automatically, both when a device is found via scan_ble() / scan_cdc() and via get_connected_devices() , and hands you
back the right subclass: BLE — from the advertised name: it contains "Mudra Pro" or "Mudra Ultimate" ( MudraModel.from_ble_name ). USB-CDC — both models share one USB VID/PID, so the SDK probes the
ports instead: a CDC? handshake tells the CONFIG port from the DATA port, and a TSYNC? probe tells Mudra Pro from Mudra Ultimate. The same physical device seen over BLE and over USB shows up as two
separate MudraDevice objects (one keyed by BLE address, one by USB
serial). Check device.MODEL (a MudraModel.PRO / MudraModel.ULTIMATE value) if your code
needs to branch on it — most callers don’t, since the shared API covers
everything but the extras below. Firmware compatibility ¶ This SDK version ( 0.5.1 ) supports: Model Firmware Mudra Pro 2.0.2.6 Mudra Ultimate 1.0.3.9 Keep your devices on these versions — other firmware versions aren’t
supported by this SDK release. The same versions are available
programmatically in supported_firmware.json at the root of the SDK. Versions are written the way the SDK reports them: major.minor.patch.tweak (the fields of FirmwareVersion ).
To read a device’s version, call await device.get_firmware_version() ; the
reply arrives through the set_on_firmware_version_received callback, and
afterwards device.get_firmware_version_info().version_string returns it
(e.g. "2.0.2.5" ). Update a device’s firmware over USB with the SDK’s DFU
support — see CONNECTION.md §6 . No finger IMU on Mudra Pro — Mudra Pro firmware has no finger (ring)
IMU: those pins are used by the SD-card slot. Enabling the finger IMU
( F_IMU ) or querying its status reports an error through the
command-error callback instead of streaming — BtCmdStatus.ERR_STATE over
BLE, BtCmdStatus.ERR_UNKNOWN over USB-CDC. What differs ¶ Mudra Pro Mudra Ultimate EMG channels 3 ( EMG_CHANNEL_COUNT = 3 ) 8 ( EMG_CHANNEL_COUNT = 8 ) EMG AFE ADS1293 ADS1298 EMG ODR enum ProEMGODR — 200/400/800/1600/2133/3200/4267/6400 Hz UltimateEMGODR — 500/1000/2000/4000 Hz Packet-loss test mode set_emg_test_mode / set_h_imu_test_mode / set_f_imu_test_mode / set_ppg_h_test_mode / set_ppg_f_test_mode — firmware-side counter overlay per sensor (see SENSORS.md §4 ) Same methods; needs firmware newer than 1.0.3.8 EMG bench self-test Not present set_emg_test(mode) (input-mux self-test: normal / test signal / inputs shorted / temp sensor / supply monitor), set_emg_channel_mask(mask) , set_emg_rld(enable) , emg_isolate() — see mudra_sdk/models/mudra_ultimate.py Host clock-sync / link stats Not present get_tsync() (echoes the firmware’s 64-bit GRTC cycle counter), get_linkstats() (BLE notification-drop stats + connection params, BLE-only) — both replies currently appear only in the SDK’s debug log; no callback receives them device.EMG_ODR_ENUM always points at the right enum for whichever model device actually is, so generic code can pick a rate without an isinstance check: odr = device . EMG_ODR_ENUM . from_value ( 800 ) # None if this model has no 800 Hz rate (Ultimate) if odr is not None : await device . set_emg_odr ( odr ) Shared sensors ¶ Both models expose the same five sensor streams (PPG as two: hand PPG_H and
finger/ring PPG_F , sharing one PPG chip), IMU/PPG config ranges, and
license-gated feature set — see the key enums quick reference for the full table (IMU ODR/accel/gyro ranges, PPG ODR, EMG
resolution). Format / Bytes per sample below describe the raw wire encoding (before
the native parser scales it into the samples: list[float] your callback
receives — see data_format.md for that shape). Both are
runtime-configurable, so treat these as defaults, not fixed values. Sensor FirmwareDataType SensorTypes Format Bytes/sample EMG emg EMG channels × (i16 or i24), per EmgRes 6/9 B (Mudra Pro, 3 ch) · 16/24 B (Mudra Ultimate, 8 ch) Hand IMU imuH H_IMU 6 × i16 ( ax,ay,az,gx,gy,gz ) 12 B (fixed) Finger IMU imuF F_IMU 6 × i16 ( ax,ay,az,gx,gy,gz ) 12 B (fixed) Hand PPG ppgH PPG_H 2 × i24 ( ch0,ch1 ) 6 B (fixed) Finger PPG ppgF PPG_F 2 × i24 ( ch0,ch1 ) 6 B (fixed) Transports ¶ Both models connect over either transport, unified behind the same API (see CONNECTION.md ): BLE — advertised name containing "Mudra Pro" or "Mudra Ultimate" . USB-CDC — USB VID/PID 0x2FE3 / 0x0001 (shared by both models), two
serial ports ( CONFIG + DATA ) told apart with a CDC? handshake; a TSYNC? probe identifies the model (see Model detection ).
Firmware update (DFU) is USB-CDC only. Status LED ¶ Both models drive a single RGB status LED through a priority-based state
machine in the device firmware. Several states can be active at once; the highest-priority active state owns the LED . This SDK doesn’t wrap it in a
typed method — see “Controlling it” below — so the tables here describe the firmware’s behavior, not this SDK’s
own code. Brightness is capped at 10% of the PWM duty cycle; RGB below is (R, G, B) ,
each 0–100 as a percentage of that cap — (0, 100, 0) is full-intensity
green at the 10% ceiling, not the LED’s absolute maximum. Mudra Pro ¶ Listed highest priority first: State ID Priority Color (R,G,B) Animation Shown when ERROR 9 255 (100, 0, 0) red constant a fault is signalled DFU_ACTIVE 10 80 (100, 0, 100) purple pulse a firmware update (MCUmgr/SMP) is uploading — see CONNECTION.md §6 STARTUP 1 75 (50, 100, 85) white one-shot fade boot (runs to completion before lower states) BATTERY_FULL 8 70 (0, 10, 100) blue+green constant charger attached, charge complete CHARGING 7 60 (0, 10, 100) blue+green pulse charging STREAMING 6 50 (0, 100, 100) teal constant a sensor is streaming data SENSOR_ON 5 40 (0, 100, 0) green constant a sensor is on but not streaming ADVERTISING 4 30 (100, 100, 0) yellow pulse BLE advertising (not connected) IDLE 3 15 (0, 100, 0) green pulse idle / connected, nothing active CUSTOM 2 10 caller-set const / pulse / blink / one-shot app drives it (see below) Mudra Ultimate ¶ Same state machine and priorities, except : no DFU_ACTIVE (this
firmware has no DFU/MCUmgr LED hook), and what Mudra Pro calls a single ERROR state is split into two: State ID Priority Color (R,G,B) Animation Shown when CHARGE_FAULT 9 72 (100, 0, 0) red constant charger attached but refusing to charge BATTERY_LOW 10 55 (100, 0, 0) red pulse battery SOC ≤ 15% (clears at ≥ 20%, hysteresis) CHARGE_FAULT outranks BATTERY_FULL (70) so a refused charge can’t read
as a finished one, but stays below STARTUP (75). BATTERY_LOW outranks STREAMING (50) so a capture that’s about to be cut short says so, but sits
below CHARGING / BATTERY_FULL (60/70) — a charger being attached takes
precedence over the low-battery warning, by construction of the priority
table rather than a special case at every call site. Every other state
( STARTUP 75, BATTERY_FULL 70, CHARGING 60, STREAMING 50, SENSOR_ON 40, ADVERTISING 30, IDLE 15, CUSTOM 10) is identical to
Mudra Pro’s table above, including IDs. Two pairs share a color on both models and differ only by animation +
priority: CHARGING vs BATTERY_FULL (blue+green; pulse vs. constant)
and IDLE vs SENSOR_ON (green; pulse vs. constant) — Mudra Ultimate
adds a third, CHARGE_FAULT vs BATTERY_LOW (red; constant vs. pulse). Controlling it (raw commands only) ¶ This SDK exposes the LED only as raw, untyped commands — there’s no MudraDevice.set_led(...) / get_led_state() method. Send these with await device.send_command(...) over BLE, built from the matching ProFirmwareCommand / UltimateFirmwareCommand member ( BT_CMD_LED / 0x60 on the wire), or as an ASCII line over USB-CDC with await Mudra().send_cdc_command(device, "LED_STATE 3") — see CONNECTION.md §4 : Command CDC token Payload Notes ledSetState LED_STATE 1 byte: state_id state_id is the raw enum ordinal from the table above — any state can be forced this way, not just CUSTOM ledClrState LED_CLR 1 byte: state_id Clears that state’s vote; another active state (or none) then shows ledRgb LED_RGB r, g, b, anim (4 bytes, each 0–100 / anim code) Sets CUSTOM ; firmware stashes every other currently-active state first so the custom color is actually visible, and restores them on LED_OFF ledBlink LED_BLINK r, g, b, count (4 bytes; count = 0 is infinite) Same stash/restore behavior as ledRgb ledOff LED_OFF (none) Clears CUSTOM and restores whatever was stashed — pair every finite ledBlink with this, or the stashed states stay cleared ledGet LED? (none) Replies with 1 byte: the currently displayed (highest-priority active) state_id , not necessarily whatever you last set What it looks like ¶ Close-ups of the status LED in the states shared by both models — the
renders are zoomed to the LED recess; the rest of the band is cropped away.
Pulsing states animate. ( DFU_ACTIVE , CHARGE_FAULT , and BATTERY_LOW have no photographed render yet; CUSTOM has no fixed look, so it isn’t
shown either.) ERROR constant STARTUP fade BATTERY_FULL constant CHARGING pulse STREAMING constant SENSOR_ON constant ADVERTISING pulse IDLE pulse The swatch dots are indicative; the precise per-channel values are in the
tables above. The state_id values are the ID column of the state tables above. The
numeric anim codes accepted by ledRgb are not documented here — they’re
defined by the device firmware, not by this SDK. License tiers ¶ Every device enforces a capability tier — FREE , PLUS , PRO ( LicenseTier in mudra_sdk.models.enums ) — via a signed token, independent
of hardware model: Higher tiers unlock faster ODRs, wider EMG resolution, and extra ranges. SD-card recording ( SENSORS.md §5 )
requires PRO specifically — starting a recording on FREE / PLUS is
rejected with BtCmdStatus.ERR_LICENSE . See AUTH.md for how a tier gets onto a device in the first place —
connecting never requires an account, but reaching anything above FREE usually does. Platform support (host side) ¶ The native MudraSDK library ships prebuilt for: Platform Architectures Windows x64 (64-bit Python required) macOS arm64, x86_64 Linux x86_64, aarch64 See native_library.md for how these are built and what
happens if one is missing for your platform.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Troubleshooting ¶ Common problems when integrating against the SDK, and how to resolve them.
If something here doesn’t cover your case, SDK_USAGE.md and
the guide pages it links to explain the design in more depth. Nothing happens after calling a get_* / set_* method ¶ Almost everything in this SDK is fire-and-forget — the reply comes back
asynchronously through a registered callback, not the coroutine’s return
value. Register the callback before triggering the request if you need to
be sure not to miss it. See SENSORS.md §6 and CALLBACKS.md . Sensor data never arrives ¶ You didn’t register a streaming callback. Setting set_on_emg_ready / set_on_imu_h_ready / set_on_imu_f_ready / set_on_ppg_h_ready / set_on_ppg_f_ready to a non- None function is the enable action — there’s no separate
“power on” call. See SENSORS.md §1 . The connection actually failed. await device.connect() never raises
— a failure is reported through on_mudra_device_connection_failed . Check await Mudra().is_connected(device) after connect() returns before
enabling sensors. You enabled sensors from on_mudra_device_connected . That callback
fires as soon as the link opens, before the SDK finishes its connect
sequence (BLE: notifications subscribed; CDC: initial status queries and START ). Enable sensors after await device.connect() has returned
instead. On CDC you never send START yourself — the SDK sends it inside connect() . See SDK_USAGE.md §4 . You reconnected the same MudraDevice object. Disconnecting (expected
or not) clears every streaming/status/storage/error/ping callback — you
must re-register them after reconnecting. See CALLBACKS.md §3 . Config change (ODR/resolution/range) seems to do nothing, or corrupts the stream ¶ set_*_odr / set_*_res /range calls don’t stop the sensor for you — the
firmware doesn’t either. Disable the sensor
( set_on_<sensor>_ready(None) ), change config, then re-enable it if it was
running. Over USB-CDC the firmware may reject a config change on a running
sensor outright — it arrives on the command-error callback as BtCmdStatus.ERR_BUSY . See SENSORS.md §3 . Streaming works, but at a lower tier than expected ¶ Connecting to a device never requires an account — a signed-out app
still streams fine, at whatever tier the device already holds (usually FREE ). Nothing raises if you skip sign-in, so this fails silently: Call auth.sign_in_email(...) before connecting. While signed in,
the SDK provisions the license tier (and user_id) itself on every connect,
and LicenseManager renews the license before it expires — renewal also
needs the sign-in, so it stops once you’re signed out. If you sign in after the device is already connected, call await auth.provision_device(device) (and await auth.provision_user_id(device) )
yourself, or reconnect. Both are no-ops while signed out. The sign-in itself is per process: after a restart, call sign_in_email(...) again before provisioning does anything. Read the device’s actual tier back via set_on_license_device_info_received rather than assuming sign-in success
implies the device got provisioned — the two are asynchronous and
independent. See AUTH.md for the full checklist. SD recording rejected with ERR_LICENSE or ERR_STATE ¶ ERR_LICENSE — SD-card recording requires the device’s PRO tier; FREE / PLUS are rejected without touching any sensor. See supported_devices.md . ERR_STATE — set_user_id(...) was never sent. This is normally
automatic (sent right after connecting, if signed in — see AUTH.md ); this fires if
the device connected while signed out. Sign in and reconnect, or call set_user_id(...) yourself. See SENSORS.md §5 . On CDC — every SD/storage call reports BtCmdStatus.ERR_UNKNOWN immediately; there is no SD storage protocol over CDC at all, by design. The native library won’t load ¶ Symptom: a log warning (“Could not load native library: …”) right after
constructing Mudra() . Mudra() itself still constructs, but the library
is required for any device work : every MudraDevice raises RuntimeError("Native library is not loaded") when it’s created (so scans
find nothing), and command encoding, sensor-data parsing and get_json_recording() all depend on it. Only cloud calls ( mudra_sdk.auth and the cloud client) work without it. Check that a prebuilt binary exists for your platform/arch under mudra_sdk/libs/<platform>/<arch>/ . On Windows, use 64-bit Python — only windows/x64 is built and
supported. See supported_devices.md for the supported list, and native_library.md for how
it’s built. Firmware update ( start_dfu ) fails ¶ DfuError mid-flow — its .stage / .message identify which step
failed (connect / upload / mark / reset). MCUboot swaps and boots the new
image on its own after reset; there’s no device-side “update complete”
push, so reconnect afterward to confirm the new version actually landed. DfuError is a subclass of RuntimeError , so catch it first if you
handle both. Plain RuntimeError before anything starts — either device has no CDC
identity (DFU is USB-only, no BLE transport exists on either product yet)
or the SDK couldn’t find a third USB-CDC SMP port on the device (it needs
DFU-enabled firmware already running). FileNotFoundError / OSError — the firmware image path is wrong or
unreadable. See CONNECTION.md §6 . LSL consumers can’t see the streams ¶ MudraLslBridge.start() returned and bridge.streams lists the streams, but
LabRecorder / pylsl.resolve_streams() on another machine shows nothing: Firewall / several network interfaces. liblsl finds streams over UDP
multicast and sends data over TCP — both must be allowed, on the interface
that actually reaches the other machine. This is by far the most common
cause and has nothing to do with the bridge. Check on the publishing
machine first ( python -c "import pylsl; print(pylsl.resolve_streams(2.0))" ). ImportError: mudra_sdk.lsl needs pylsl — install the optional
dependency: pip install pylsl . On Linux, also install liblsl itself. RuntimeError: none of the requested sensors reported status — no
sensor answered its status query within status_timeout (default 3 s).
Start the bridge only after await device.connect() has returned and await Mudra().is_connected(device) is true (not from on_mudra_device_connected , which fires before the device is set up), and
give the first status replies a moment; raise status_timeout on a slow
link (see “Sensor data never arrives” above). A stream went quiet after you registered your own callback — the
bridge uses the set_on_*_ready slot of every sensor it publishes; read
the samples back from LSL instead. See LSL.md §4 . Streams went quiet after the device reconnected — a disconnect clears
the bridge’s callbacks; call bridge.start() again. See LSL.md §6 . bleak / smpclient import errors when installing ¶ bleak is pinned to the wearable-devices fork’s develop branch, not upstream PyPI bleak — make sure you installed from mudra_sdk/requirements.txt rather than a stray pip install bleak . git must be on your PATH , with access to that fork, for the install to succeed.
